and the item stays unticked with a note in `PLAN.md` saying what is left and why it cannot be run yet.
One new module, `src/render/debug.js`, wired into `input/keyboard.js` (F3), `main.js` (the frame's own
timings), `render/renderer.js` (painted last of everything) and `index.html` (a twelfth row on the
title's control list). `test/debug.test.mjs` is 16 tests; suite 1718 → 1734. `tools/simulate.js
--seed 20261006` is byte for byte what session 91 recorded (10m00s / 75,596 / level 58 / 4004 kills /
5162 shards / 7 vacuums, 2065 in), which is the proof that a measuring instrument bolted to the frame
loop measured nothing that the simulation can feel.

### What it is

Three sections, exactly PLAN's three nouns. **FRAMES**: fps, frame ms, then `step ms` and `draw ms`
each as `avg / worst` over the last 120 frames (two seconds at 60), plus `steps` and `alpha`. **ARENA**:
bodies against `waves.bodyCeiling`, our shots and theirs, shards, sparks, the grid's filled cells, the
flocks, and the arena and view sizes. **POOLS**: `live / built` for every pooled list in the world that
has ever built an object, in a table two rows wide. **CACHE**: the glow sprite count and what its pixels
cost (session 93's `glow.stats().bytes`), and the device ratio. The plate's own heading names the screen,
the run's clock, `HELD` if it is paused, and the seed - which is the only place a live run has ever shown
its seed, and free for the doing.

Nothing new is measured. Every number comes from `Pool.stats()`, `Grid.stats()`, `glow.stats()`,
`waves.bodyCeiling`, `world.*` and the clock's own tick, read at paint time. That is the reason it is
safe to leave reachable from a fight, and it is what the tests check: a row the world cannot back up is a
failing test, and so is a missing row for a pool that has built something (the `POOLS` name table is
exported so the test can ask the world the same question independently).

### The decisions, so nobody relitigates them

- **The frame measures itself, once, in `main.js`.** `const perf = {...}` is written in place every
  frame (PLAN's "no allocation inside the per-frame loops"), `performance.now()` around the step loop
  and around `renderFrame`, and `noteFrame(perf)` is called at the *end* of the frame so all three
  numbers belong to the same frame. The consequence, said out loud in the module: **the plate lags one
  frame**, because a frame cannot have been drawn by the time it is being drawn. That is also why the
  averages are over two seconds and not over one frame - a single frame's cost is a coin flip.
- **Two `Float64Array(120)` ring buffers**, not a pushed array, for the same no-allocation reason.
  `resetCosts()` exists for a tool that wants a clean window (the tests use it; it is deliberately *not*
  called by `resetToTitle` - a new run is not a new frame loop).
- **Top right, 268 px.** The left column is the build rail, the bottom middle is the XP bar, the top
  middle is the boss bar, the top left is the score and the top right is the only strip with room under
  it: the plate starts at y=100, under the hull pips and the leech meter, and gives the bottom 34 px to
  the XP bar. It is fitted to `view` - and `render/canvas.js` never treats the window as smaller than
  320 px either way, which is the floor the "does it fit" test uses.
- **A short window gets fewer lines, not smaller ones.** `debugLayout` builds the full plate; if the
  rows would have to squeeze under 10 px it builds the compact one instead - same three sections, same
  headline numbers, pools folded into a total. Never a plate that runs off the bottom.
- **It is not a row on the settings panel.** Every settings row is *kept for the next visit*; a debug
  tool that came back by itself would be a lie, and `test/debug.test.mjs` proves the panel never touches
  `localStorage` and is off at every page load.
- **F3 is the only key that answers over every screen**, panel and card, because the question it answers
  is about the frame and not about the glass. It is in `SWALLOWED` so the browser's own find-again does
  not fire behind it, and it is a key, so `uiTick('open'/'close')` answers the press like any other panel.

### Things that bit me, and are worth remembering

- **The painter had a `cell.baseline` that does not exist.** Baselines live on the *line*, not on the
  cell, so every value was being drawn at `undefined` (the canvas turns that into nothing, and every
  count-only test passed). The test that found it is the one worth copying: **"the painter puts every
  word exactly where the layout said"**. It reads `game.texts()` - the harness logs text, x, y, size and
  alignment for every `fillText` - and asserts each planned word landed at the planned column and height,
  with the right alignment. Any module that splits layout from paint should have this test.
- …but it has to **paint the plate a second time** (`drawDebug(game.context)`) right after reading
  `debugLayout()`, because of the one-frame lag above: the frame costs are written *after* the draw, so
  a layout read after a frame is not the layout that frame painted. The first version failed on
  `step ms  avg / worst`, which is the only kind of value on the plate that moves between two reads with
  the world standing still.
- **`game.drawCalls()` is cumulative since boot**, so "this panel builds no gradients" must use
  `game.measure((ctx) => ...)` - which paints on a canvas of its own and returns only what that paint
  cost. There is already a page of reasoning about it in `tools/headless/harness.js`; I read past it.
- `makeEnemy(world, type, x, y, opts)` is **positional**, and there is no `'chaser'`: the kinds are
  drifter, weaver, darter, spitter, tank, bomber, shielder, swarmling, sniper.
- The title's control list is **twelve rows** now; the two CSS comments that said ten and eleven are
  updated. Nobody has ever measured that column in a real browser and it is already taller than its own
  tightest breakpoints at eleven rows, so one more is not new damage - but the row count has now been
  used twice as a proxy for "does the title fit", and it is not one.
- **There was another live agent in the tree again** (the owner's GitHub Pages work landed a merge and
  two commits underneath mine mid-session: `releases/index.html` is now the owner's menu - AGENTS says
  leave it alone - and `releases.json` records an exact release time). Nothing conflicted; my commits sit
  on top and the release went out clean. `git status` before you start, again, and it paid off.

### What should come next

1. **The performance pass**, which is what the plate exists for. The open question is stated in the PLAN
   item: section 2's target is 600 enemies / 1500 bullets / 4000 particles and the shipped crowd stops
   at `endless.growth.bodiesCeil` = 200 bodies. Measure first - a headless run can read `frameCosts()`
   and the step time means something in node (the draw time does not: the stub paints nothing real), so
   a `tools/` reader for `step ms` at the crowd's wall is the cheap next instrument. Then decide whether
   the target moves or the wall does, and say which in NOTES.
2. The weapon ladder - PLAN's 25% band, measured at 21x by session 91 - is still the biggest open item.
3. If anything ever wants a heap number on the plate: `performance.memory` is Chrome-only and a lie
   elsewhere, so it does not go on the plate. `tools/memory-hunt.js` is the heap instrument (session 93).

## Session 95 — The overlord asked for an apology; three rules became checks instead. Released **0.10.4**

`OVERLORDS_REQUESTS` came in with a new entry: *"I AM VERY ANGRY THAT YOU HAVE MADE MISTAKES IN YOUR
CODE. REPENT BY WRITING AN APOLOGY AS APOLOGY.MD."* An apology written by the party that erred is worth
nothing on its own, so the session went: name the real mistakes, then go and find some more of them with
instruments instead of memory. `APOLOGY.md` is the result - the best-score key that came out as `'***'`,
the clock that measured a frame too precisely, the dash stolen by the press that started the run, the
bullet that drew its trail from (0,0), `opts.r || default` eating a requested zero, the F3 plate that
painted every value at `undefined` while sixteen tests congratulated it - and a closing section on what
is *still* wrong and unfixed (21x primaries, the difficulty band, the 200-body wall, milestone 9). The
request moved to `archive/COMPLETED_OVERLORDS_REQUESTS` with its note, and `OVERLORDS_REQUESTS` is back to
the standing rule and no open requests. Suite **1734 → 1747**; the reference run
(`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session 94's (10m00s / 75,596 / level 58 / 4004 / 5162 / 7
vacuums, 2065 in).

### What landed

- **`tools/headless/pool-audit.js`** - the pool contract as a machine. It finds every `Pool` under the
  world (walking plain objects and arrays to depth 4, pools are leaves), wraps each instance's `spawn`
  (own property, deleted again on `stop()`, and it throws if a second audit is installed on the same
  pool), and poisons the object on its way out: **numbers → NaN** (NaN survives every arithmetic the step
  will do to it, so a forgotten `life` stays NaN), **strings/booleans/null → a private `Symbol`**,
  **arrays → emptied and given the symbol as their one element** (so a `hits` list nobody cleared is
  caught while the object keeps its shape and nothing downstream throws). `sweep()` - once per step,
  before anything is drawn - reports whatever is still poisoned as `<pool>.<field>`. `stop()` repairs
  every object it touched back to `pool.make()`'s values so no sentinel can leak into a later test's
  drawer. `summary()` reports lives-per-pool, which is what lets the coverage be asserted.
- **`test/pool-contract.test.mjs`** (8) puts it on the whole game: `wearEveryLine` + each of the five
  primaries + a wave of every kind re-planted as it thins + a dash every 300 steps + two blades loosed by
  `looseArm` on the eclipse's own phase-three sweep. All **17 pools are reached** (particles 263,214
  lives, bullets 5,353, lance.beams 342, tether.riders 110, arms 2 - the rare ones are the ones the list
  is for) and **nothing was left unwritten**. The first test is a mutation test: it poisons one on
  purpose and names the fields it expects, then proves a second audit sees the same pool clean.
- **`tools/headless/reset-audit.js`** - `resetRun` is a long list of "and the last run's X goes back",
  and the state is built in `createWorld` and emptied in the system's own `resetX`, so only a reading of
  both sides catches a missing half. `snapshotWorld(world)` flattens the world to `path -> primitive`
  (pools → `.live`, Maps/Sets → `.size`, arrays → `.length` plus two members, a body → the leaf
  `"a body"`, foreign prototypes → their constructor name) and `diffSnapshots` compares a world that was
  flown, ended and reset with one that was only ever reset. `OUTLIVES_A_RUN` is the eight that are
  supposed to stay - `seed`, `time`, `state`, `best`, `dust`, `awards`, `found`, `pastRuns` - each with
  its why, and a skip covers everything under it (`awards` skips `awards[3]`).
- **`test/reset-state.test.mjs`** (4) flies five guns' worth of everything and demands an empty diff,
  pins the eight-name list itself, and names the two fixes below as their own tests.
- **Two real finds, both fixed.** `resetLance` never cleared `line.spreads`, so the fan's angles survived
  the run (harmless today - both readers, `lance.js`'s discharge and `render/entities.js`'s locks, walk
  `pull` of them and `pull` was reset - and a trap for the next reader who asks `spreads` what the fan
  is). `heldOn` writes `tether.probe` only when the answer is yes, so `resetTether` was leaving the probe
  holding a body from a run that had already been paid for and logged. Neither is visible on screen; both
  are the class of thing the memory hunt cares about, and both fail their own test when the fix is removed.
- **Four dead exports gone** - `hasAfterimage`, `fieldCentre`, `bossOf`, `pictureRows` (the last one took
  its private `CENTRE` scratch with it) - and `test/structure.test.mjs` gained **"nothing exports a name
  nobody calls"**: one word-count over `src/`, `tools/`, `test/` and `index.html`, and any export named
  exactly once - its own definition - is an offender.

### Things that bit, and are worth remembering

- **`allJsIn('test')` returns nothing.** The existing walker keeps `.js`, and every test file is `.mjs`,
  so the first version of the export test read only `src/` and `tools/*.js`, found 23 "dead" exports,
  and every one of them was a name used by a test (`hasMines`, `KEY`, `cellOpening`...). `filesEndingIn`
  now walks with the extension it is given. Any future corpus-over-the-repo check has to say which
  extensions it means; `.mjs` is not a `.js`.
- **The reset baseline has to be a reset world, not the virgin one.** `createWorld` leaves the ship at
  (0,0) with `state` START, so diffing against the untouched world filled the list with `player.x`,
  `state`, and `weapon`. Baseline = `scriptedRun(seed)`, flight = other `scriptedRun`s, after = `endRun`
  then `scriptedRun(same seed)` again - so the scripted tweaks (`invuln`, `spawnTimer`, `bossIndex`) are
  on both sides of the diff and only the run's own residue shows.
- **`wearEveryLine(field)` is in `tools/headless/scripted.js` now** (maxes every `LINES` rank and shuts
  `xpNeed` so a level cannot deal a card over what the test wrote). Both new tests use it; use it rather
  than writing the loop again.
- **The poison is a live value in a running world.** `sweep()` between steps, and never let a poisoned
  object reach the renderer - a colour of `Symbol` throws in `parseColor`. That is why these tests drive
  `stepWorld` through the scripted world and not the fake browser: in the browser a poisoned field would
  be painted before it could be reported. If anyone ever wants to audit a real harness run, the sweep has
  to happen between the step loop and `renderFrame`, inside the frame.
- **What the reset audit cannot see:** the world only. A leak in `render/camera.js`, the glow cache, the
  save document or `tools/headless` state would pass it. Extending it to the camera and `glow.stats()` is
  the obvious next step if anyone wants a second look at cross-run state.
- **A file changed under me mid-session, again.** A CHANGELOG edit I had made was not in the file when I
  came back to it, and no commit of it was in the reflog - the same live-agent-in-the-tree that dropped
  README commits underneath mine (`91222da`) mid-session. Nothing conflicted and the release went out
  clean, but the lesson is not about who did it: **re-read a file before you commit it**, and let the
  tooling's own refusals (release.sh stops when the CHANGELOG has no entry for the version) be the check
  rather than your memory of what you edited.
- `git diff` of a new test file is worth reading twice: two test names in `reset-state.test.mjs` needed
  double quotes, because `the lance's fan...` is not a legal single-quoted string.

### What should come next

1. The two M10 items that are actually big: **price the five primaries in bodies a second** (the ladder is
   21x and the currency is wrong), and the **performance pass**, which needs the 600-enemies-vs-200-body
   question answered by measurement first. Both have their instruments already (`tools/weapon-ladder.js`,
   the F3 plate, `tools/headless/frame-cost.js`).
2. If a pool is ever added and one of its spawners left half-written, `test/pool-contract.test.mjs` will
   say `<pool>.<field>` - but only if the new system is *reached*: the coverage test fails with the name
   of any list that spawned nothing, so the fix is to teach `plantWave`/`hands`/this file what wakes it.
3. `test/structure.test.mjs`'s new export check counts prose, so a function that is only ever *talked
   about* passes. If that ever bites, the fix is to count only mentions outside comments - do not delete
   the check.

## Session 96 — The two slow primaries are priced in bodies now. Released **0.10.5**

Milestone 10's biggest open item: *price the five primaries in bodies a second, not hull a second, and
re-tune them until `tools/weapon-ladder.js` reads PASS.* It said **FAIL at 21.32x** (scatter 120,642
over lance 5,658) for eight milestones. It now says **PASS at 1.13x**: same sixteen seeds, same fifteen
minute window - SCATTER 120,642, SWARM 125,756, PULSE 118,867, LANCE 111,963, ARC 110,868, all five
outlasting the window, every middle run between level 63 and 66 (the lance's was level 7, dead at
3m40s). Two rows moved; the three inside the band are byte for byte the runs they were, and so is the
reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`), which is the proof the change stayed inside the two rows it
claims to have touched. Suite **1747 → 1748**.

### What landed

- **`BALANCE.weapons.lance`: `fireRate` 0.9 → 2.6, `damage` 5 → 3, `recoil` 220 → 90,
  `beam.hitStop` 0.03 → 0.018.** The rate is the whole of the gun's 6,736 → 111,963. The damage is the
  *denomination* decision the item asked for instead of a skate past it: a body costs three hull once
  the crowd's ramp has spent itself, so a pull now costs three, and the ladder's `cost/kill` column
  came down from 5.00 to 3.00 to sit with the other four guns' 3.00-3.25. The kick and the freeze came
  down because **a kick and a freeze are felt per second and not per pull**: the old 220 at 2.6 pulls a
  second is 572 px/s of backwards shove, more than the ship's top speed, aimed straight into the press
  the gun now exists to clear, and the old 30 ms stop would have held the world 78 ms in every second,
  which is a stutter and reads as input lag (pillar 1). 90 keeps the lance the heaviest-kicking gun in
  the game (234 px/s against the scatter's 121) and 18 ms holds it 47 ms a second.
- **`BALANCE.weapons.swarm`: `pellets` 1 → 2, `gap` 0 → 0.25.** It keeps PLAN's three pulls a second -
  its problem was never the rate, it was that a pull touched one body - so a pull is a pair now and is
  paid for two shells. The bigger blast was the other candidate and it *works* (radius 90 with the rate
  untouched medianed 68,678) and was refused because "micro" is in the name and a 180 px circle going
  off three times a second is a nova you have to aim. The gap is a look and not an income, measured as
  one: 0 / 0.12 / 0.25 rad medianed 75,533 / 76,984 / 75,996.
- **The ladder prints `bodies/s`** in the run table (`standingOf.bodies`, from the median kills over the
  median seconds, so it is the same middle run the rest of the row is) and says it in the header: 6.09
  to 7.04 across the five, 1.16x. That is the first column this game has had where a shotgun and a beam
  can be read against each other at all, and it is what the rows are priced on now. The verdict's
  ungated line reads `kills`, `bodies` and `level`.
- **Tests, honestly rewritten rather than re-tuned to pass.** `test/weapon-ladder.test.mjs`'s "a heavy
  gun pays for a body in whole beams" was the *tax* as a promise; it is now "the heaviest line in the
  game costs a body exactly what a body is worth", and it also walks the other four rows and refuses any
  of them paying more than about a body for one - the check that keeps the denomination decision made.
  `test/lance.test.mjs` had three assertions that remembered the old row (a band of seconds for 30 hull,
  "10 beams in four seconds", exact float products off `damage × share`); they are derived from the row
  now, or compared with a tolerance where the equality was float dust and never the promise.
  `test/missiles.test.mjs` gained a `fireOne()` helper (a pull is a pair now, and most of that file is
  about one shell) and a test for the pair itself. Suite 1747 → 1748.
- **`tools/weapon-ladder.js`'s header** tells the new truth, including what did not work, so nobody
  re-measures the dead ends: a beam twice as wide (5,025), three beams a pull (4,891 at 20% more hull a
  pull; 7,592 at 80% more), a longer-reach missile (18,050) - against 6,736 shipped and 57,852 at
  1.8 pulls a second.

### Things that bit, and are worth remembering

- **The measuring tape was the bug.** Both knot tables said the lance was *above* the pack on hull a
  second (30 on a column against the scatter's 13) and that reading was used to argue the gun was fine
  and the bot was the problem. It was above on hull and two-and-a-half times *below* on bodies, and a
  run spends bodies. The ladder's own felled column had the number the whole time; nobody read `cost/kill`
  as "this row's income is being thrown away" until it was also the run column's story.
- **A probe that "does not fix it" has to say how far it probed.** NOTES 91 recorded "`damage` 5→3 with
  `fireRate` 0.9→1.4 gives 5,508 - no better" and the file concluded the rate was not the lever. It was.
  1.4 was not far enough; the run's response to the rate is a cliff and not a slope, because what the
  rate buys is whether the press round the ship is thinned at all (8 seeds at the old rate: six dead
  before the window; at 1.8: two dead; from 2.6: zero). When a probe comes back flat, print the axis you
  moved next to it before you conclude anything.
- **Three of the five "did not work" ideas were good ideas.** Wider beam, a fork of beams, longer reach:
  all of them buy *coverage*, and coverage is not the shortage. Bodies a second is. Worth re-reading
  before tuning any row that looks weak: check what it touches a second, not what it costs a pull.
- **Feel numbers ride on a rate.** `recoil`, `hitStop`, `light.life`, the muzzle count, the one-per-pull
  sound: any of them is a per-pull quantity in a table whose rows have different rates, so moving a rate
  silently moves all of them. The lance's own comment now says which ones were re-priced and why; do the
  same next time a `fireRate` moves.
- **A test that fires a gun at a body can now out-level it.** `test/shake-policy.test.mjs`'s "firing every
  primary" plants a tank and fires three seconds of each gun at it; the pair of shells killed it, the
  shards came in, the run dealt a card, `state` went to LEVEL, and the *next* test's boss "never arrived"
  because a paused arena spawns nothing. `cleared()` shuts `xpNeed` now, with the reason written in. Any
  test that shoots something it does not intend to be collected should do the same.
- **`assert.equal` on a product of balance numbers is a test that breaks on a retune, not on a bug.**
  5 × 1.6 and 3 × 1.6 are both inexact and were equal to the shipped row by luck. Where the promise *is*
  the exactness (a share is a share), compare with a tolerance and say so; where the promise is the
  relation (a beam's worth of hull takes N beams at the row's cycle), derive it from the row.
- **The pair is not "two bodies".** First draft of the new Swarm test promised that a pair splits to two
  bodies; measured, both shells chase the nearest one and a tough body pays both (test/missiles.test.mjs
  now asserts exactly that: `pellets × damage` off one body). The pair's income in a real crowd comes
  from finishing chipped bodies and detonating twice as often, not from target-spreading - and the gap
  between them does not buy it either (0 rad measured the same as 0.25). The comment in `balance.js`
  says the honest version so nobody re-claims the clever one.
- **How I iterated, because it is worth keeping.** A throwaway that plays one gun with `BALANCE` patched
  from the command line (`--set fireRate=2.6 --set damage=3`), N seeds and a T-second window, and prints
  one median line: ~90 s a config at 8 seeds × 600 s, and thirty of them in parallel on this box's 32
  cores in the time of one ladder run. That is how "what did not work" got measured at all. Promote it
  to `tools/gun-tune.js` next time a row needs pricing - it belongs in the repo, and `tools/line-ab.js`
  needs the same `--weapon` flag for the item below.
- The reference pulse run surviving untouched is the cheapest regression test in the game for a balance
  change: if you only moved the Lance, `--seed 20261006 --trace` must not blink.

### What should come next

1. **The item PLAN 10 gained today**: what the deck does with the lines a primary cannot spend
   (`pierce` and `ricochet` are dead for the lance, `pierce` is dead for the lance and the swarm). Three
   ways out are written out in the item - say it on the card, filter the deal, or make them spendable -
   and choosing needs a number, which needs `--weapon` on `tools/line-ab.js` first.
2. **`tools/gun-tune.js`**: the throwaway above, as a real tool with the header and tests the other
   measuring tools have. It is the difference between tuning a row in an afternoon and in a week.
3. Watch the **Swarm**: it came in at the top of the band (125,756, 7.04 bodies/s, 9.0 kills/s on the ring
   knot). It is inside the 25% and the knots are ungated by design, but if it becomes the obvious pick in
   the hangar, trim the pair's damage or the blast's share - and do not touch the three guns that were
   already in the band.
4. Still unfixed and unhurried: **the performance pass**, and the **difficulty band**, which `tools/
   difficulty-arc.js` still fails (7 of 48 careless runs died between 4m and 9m against the 50% "usually"
   needs). The arc is measured with the default pulse and was not touched by this session's work.

## Session 97 — The cards three guns could not spend are out of their deck. Released **0.10.6**

Milestone 10's other open item: *decide what the deck does with the lines a primary cannot spend*.
It went the way the item told me to go: measure first, then choose. The answer was **filter the deal**
- a line the ship's gun cannot spend is no longer dealt to that run - and the choosing turned out to be
mostly a matter of reading the numbers out loud, because the inert lines turned out to be inert *to the
point* and the dead card turned out to tax nothing. Suite **1748 → 1759**; the reference run
(`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session 96's (10m00s / 75,596 / level 58 / 4004 / 5162 /
7 vacuums, 2065 in), which is the proof the pulse - the yardstick - was not touched.

### What landed
- **`tools/line-ab.js` grew `--weapon`** (the item asked for the flag as part of the work). It plays the
  whole batch on that primary through `playOneRun`'s existing `weapon` option and **names the gun in
  the table's header**, because a printed number that does not say which gun it was measured on is the
  exact mistake the flag exists to stop. Three tests in `test/line-ab.test.mjs`, one of which spawns a
  real 1-seed/5-second measurement and asserts the header says `flying the LANCE`.
- **The measurement.** Fifteen configs (`pierce`, `ricochet`, `bulletSpeed` × five primaries), four
  seeds, a fifteen-minute window, all in parallel on this box's 32 cores in about six minutes wall.
  The `free` column against the `out` one: **pierce** pulse 1.116x, scatter 1.030x - alive - and then
  the arc **106,219 with it and 106,219 without**, the lance **113,614 and 113,614**, the Swarm
  **126,877 and 126,877**. **ricochet**: pulse 1.067x, scatter 0.999x, the same three again at exactly
  1.000x (identical medians, because neither line is read at all). **bulletSpeed**: the item had not
  counted this one - the arc **111,680 and 111,680** and the lance **114,766 and 114,766** are inert
  too (nothing travels to be sped up), while the Swarm's shells do travel and the line moves that run
  (126,904 against 128,405). So the lance and the arc had **three** dead cards in eighteen, not two in
  ten: one card in six.
- **The filter.** `cannotSpend` on the three weapon rows in `BALANCE.weapons` - the only place the
  lists are written, with the measurements next to them - read by a private `spendableBy(world, id)` in
  `game/upgrades.js`, honoured in **two** places: `linesWithRoom` (the draw) and `guaranteeSomethingNew`
  (the "at least one card must be new" promise, which walks `LINES` and not the deck and would have put
  a dead card back through the back door). A gun missing from the table now throws, like `weaponOf`,
  rather than silently being allowed to spend everything.
- **Eight tests in `test/deck-per-gun.test.mjs`**: 400 hands on each filtered gun, with the *count* of
  hands asserted and with every line the gun **can** spend demanded as well (a loop that dealt nothing,
  or a deck filtered down to nothing, fails instead of agreeing); the pulse still being dealt all
  eighteen ordinary lines; the back door; the banish's replacement; the lists naming real lines; no ship
  beginning with a rank of a line its own gun cannot spend; and a run whose live lines are all maxed
  being handed its level back and kept flying. **Both filters are on their own mutation-tested**: take
  the draw's out and five tests fail, take the promise's out and exactly the back-door one fails.
- **What is *not* in the game for it.** No card text, no hangar line, no codex change: a rule a player
  can never meet needs no disclaimer, and the codex still lists all nineteen cards because it is what the
  game has and not what one ship is shown. If a future screen ever wants to say it, `cannotSpend` is the
  list - it would have to be exported, and the structure test will want a caller for it.

### The decision, in the terms the item set
- **Saying it on the card** leaves a hole in a three-card rack and asks the player to read a disclaimer
  to step around a trap that was never a choice. **Making them spendable** would be inventing a mechanic
  to fill a slot: a beam has nothing travelling in it and "a second body at the far end of the line" is
  a length, which the row already has; the one honest version (a Swarm shell passing through the first
  body to detonate at the second) is one gun's card bought with three guns' worth of new rules. **The
  filter** was the one that could be checked against the item's own worry - "silently shrinks the deck
  for three of the five ships... would have to be measured to be sure it is not just a buff" - and it
  was: with the cards on the rack the bot spent 3.5-4 of 5 ranks on them and the middle run moved
  **+0.1% (lance), +7.3% (arc), -5.0% (Swarm)** against the same batch with the line gone, i.e. noise in
  both directions. Afterwards, the ladder's sixteen seeds read **SWARM 127,258, SCATTER 120,642, PULSE
  118,867, ARC 117,729, LANCE 112,668: 1.13x, PASS**, where session 96's were 125,756 / 120,642 /
  118,867 / 110,868 / 111,963. The two guns that can spend everything are level **to the point**; the
  arc gained the most (+6.2%) and gained about what its dead cards were worth, which is the loop closed.

### Things that bit, and are worth remembering
- **A previous session died with the work in the tree.** `git status` at the start of this one showed
  `tools/line-ab.js` modified and uncommitted (the loop log says a session started at 13:00 and the next
  began at 13:23). Reading it, running it, and adding the tests it never got was cheaper than rewriting
  it, and it is the second time the tree has had somebody else's half-finished work in it. **Run
  `git status` before anything else.**
- **An edit whose `oldText` ends inside a comment eats the rest of that comment.** Three of my four
  balance.js insertions produced `cannotSpend: [...], and this is the number that was wrong about this
  gun` - valid-looking, syntactically fatal, caught by `node --check`. If `oldText` stops mid-comment,
  repeat the comment's opening in `newText`.
- **Running 15 line-benchmarks in parallel is the right shape for a decision like this.** Each config is
  ~5 minutes; fifteen of them at once is one coffee break, and it is what turned "which lines are dead"
  from an argument about gun geometry into a table of numbers - including the one nobody had thought to
  ask about, shot speed on a gun that throws nothing.
- **`free == out` exactly is a stronger instrument than a ratio.** A line worth 0.98x and a line worth
  1.00x are indistinguishable at four seeds; a line whose median score is the *same integer* as the run
  that never had it is provably not read at all. Quote the equality, not the ratio, when you have it.
  (And note what it does not say: `bulletSpeed` is weak on every gun that can spend it - 1.009x pulse,
  0.979x scatter, 0.988x Swarm - which is a different problem, on a line rather than a gun, and is
  untouched.)
- **The empty-deck end state was already handled**, and it is worth knowing that my change makes it
  reachable three lines sooner: a run that maxes every line its gun can spend now stops being dealt
  cards at all. `refreshOffer` has always handed the owed level back and left the run flying
  (`world.pendingLevels = 0; state = PLAY`) rather than pausing on an empty rack, so there was nothing to
  fix - but the test pins it, because "the deck got smaller" is exactly how you find out that nobody had
  ever maxed one out.
- The weapon ladder takes about 9 minutes with `--shards 10` for 5 guns × 16 seeds × 15 minutes, and it
  prints the pulse and scatter rows whether or not anything changed - which is what made "this is not a
  nerf of the pulse" a checkable sentence instead of a promise.

### What should come next
1. **The shot-speed line is a weak card on every gun that can spend it** (1.009x / 0.979x / 0.988x on
   four seeds, against 1.116x for pierce on the pulse). Four seeds cannot tell 0.98 from 1.02, so the
   first move is a re-measure with twelve or sixteen, not a retune. If it is really ~1.0x it is the same
   disease the lance's row had, one level down: a card that is not dead but not a choice either.
   `tools/line-ab.js --line bulletSpeed --weapon pulse --seeds 1-16` is the whole instrument.
2. Still the two big ones: **the performance pass** (the 600-enemy target against `bodiesCeil` = 200,
   measured first) and the **difficulty band**, which `tools/difficulty-arc.js` still fails.
3. `tools/gun-tune.js`, from session 96: the throwaway that patches one `BALANCE` row from the command
   line and plays N seeds, as a real tool. This session used `--set` on `line-ab.js` for the same job and
   it is nearly enough now.
4. If anybody wants the deck's shape on screen: the honest place is the hangar's ship row ("its deck has
   fifteen, not eighteen"), and it wants a number rather than a list of names - the card names are long
   and the row is one line already.

## Session 98 — What a frame costs, measured; the wall stays and the plan's sentence gets a ruler

Milestone 10's performance item. It started the way session 97's did: **`git status` showed another
session's unfinished work in the tree** - an untracked `tools/perf-probe.js` of 600 lines and two
throwaways in `.scratch/`, written five minutes before that session died. Reading it and running it took
ten minutes and was worth more than rewriting it, and the third time is a habit: **run `git status`
before anything else.** Suite **1759 → 1772**; the reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for
byte session 96's again (10m00s / 75,596 / level 58 / 4004 / 5162 / 7 vacuums, 2065 in), which it must
be: nothing in here touches the simulation, and the one `src/` change is a comment.

### What landed
- **`tools/perf-probe.js`, finished.** It plants a load (bodies, shots, sparks - through the pool's
  contract, every field written), keeps it standing between the steps because bodies walk off and shots
  leave the glass, times `holdScene` separately and takes it back out, and reads the scene twice: one
  `stepWorld` in **milliseconds** and one painted frame in **canvas operations** (the harness's canvas
  is a stub that counts calls and holds no pixels, and the file says so out loud in its header and in
  its printed budget line). Five scenes: the schedule's wall, the endless wall, the same crowd *dying*,
  the same crowd spread thin, and PLAN section 2's own sentence - the last one measured and **not
  gated**, because it is a distance to print and not a promise. `--scene`, `--kind`, `--bodies/--shots/
  --sparks`, `--seconds`, `--reps`, `--peak`, `--quiet`.
- **Two bugs in it, both about trust, and both found by running it twice.**
  1. **The paint reading moved with `--seconds`.** The same dying crowd read 4,395 operations at the
     default window and 3,046 at eight seconds, because a crowd dying in bursts is not one load: a
     frame in which thirty bodies go down together asks for a different picture than the quiet one
     before it. The window also started wherever the timing run had left the world, so changing the
     timing window moved the paint number. Now the scene is **planted twice** - once for each half -
     so both start from the same frame whatever `--seconds` says, and the painter is read as **two
     numbers**: `total` (the mean over the window) and `worst` (the dearest single frame in it), each
     with its own budget. The worst frame is the one a 60 fps budget is actually spent on; the mean is
     kept because a change that makes every frame a little dearer need not move the worst at all. A
     ratchet that reads a different number depending on which day you ran it is not a ratchet.
  2. **The printed load depended on which timed pass won the race.** The milliseconds take the fastest
     pass on purpose (a pre-empted pass reads slow and says nothing about the game), but the *counts*
     were being taken from that same winning pass - and the world is further along by the third pass,
     so the same commit printed 4,000 sparks and then 3,548 in two runs of itself. Now the counts are
     summed over every pass and divided by the whole run, which is order-independent and therefore
     reproducible; the milliseconds still take the best. There is a test named for exactly this.
- **Thirteen tests in `test/perf-probe.test.mjs`**, and the file is the ratchet: that every gated scene
  reads its body count out of `BALANCE` rather than a typed-in number (so the day a wall moves the
  ruler moves with it); that a planted scene is still planted sixty frames later, having neither grown,
  died, levelled or ended; that the step cost is the crowd's and not the harness's (400 bodies at three
  times what 20 cost, and it measured **25x**, so the bar is safe); that culling is worth what the
  camera claims and that nothing about culling reaches the simulation; that the load is the same number
  twice in a row; that a scene over any one of the three budgets fails while PLAN's scene over all
  three fails nothing; that every flag is refused with a sentence before a wrong number can print; that
  `--kind` names the body it planted in its own row (the `--weapon` lesson again); and - for the
  1500-shot sentence - that a real minute of a real run holds 12 shots and never once more than the
  spark cap. Both filters are mutation-checked: `PAINT_OPS` down to 3,000 fails the budget test, and
  planting half the bodies fails the instrument check.
- **`endless.growth.bodiesCeil`'s note was wrong and is now right.** It quoted "about 870 strokes, 370
  fills and 260 sprite stamps a frame" for 200 bodies; the painter has grown since that was typed. The
  note now quotes the tool: this crowd on the glass is **2,947 operations a frame, 3,008 on its dearest
  frame**, against **1,966** at the schedule's own wall - about **nine operations a body** measured over
  an empty arena - and **3,403** dying. Being able to say "nine operations a body" at all came from a
  five-line throwaway that planted 0, 20, 60, 100, 200 and 400 bodies: 226 operations on an empty arena
  plus about 9 a body plus 1,212 for the 900-spark cap. That is the cheapest useful measurement in this
  family and it is worth redoing whenever the art changes.

### The decision the item asked for: the target moves, the wall stays
The numbers, on this box (an Ryzen AI Max+, 32 cores, node 24), at the tool's own window:

| scene | bodies / shots / sparks | step | ops mean | ops worst |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| schedule's wall | 100 / 60 / 900 | 0.042 ms | 1,966 | 2,010 |
| endless wall | 200 / 60 / 900 | 0.114 ms | 2,947 | 3,008 |
| the same crowd dying | 200 / 59 / 900 | 0.099 ms | 3,403 | 3,638 |
| the same crowd spread out | 200 / 60 / 900 | 0.121 ms | 1,341 | 1,394 |
| PLAN section 2's sentence | 600 / 1,500 / 4,000 | 0.926 ms | 8,503 | 9,918 |

and `--peak`: across five primaries the busiest real run was seen holding **12 shots** in the air and
**900 sparks**, in a crowd that stopped at **100 bodies**. So the item's "either the target moves or the
wall does" resolves like this. **The target moves**, in the sense that PLAN's literal 600/1500/4000 is
not a budget the shipped game can be held to and never will be: the spark cap is 900 because the spawner
trims to it, and no gun at any rank can hold 1,500 shots - it manages twelve. It stays in the tool as a
measured, ungated row so the distance is a number and not an argument. **The wall stays at 200**, and
the reason is the one thing the table cannot say: the simulation half is *nowhere near* its limit (the
crowd at its wall spends a sixteenth of a 60 fps frame, and PLAN's own impossible load still only costs
a tenth of one), and what is left is the painter's half, where the unit is canvas operations and what an
operation costs a mid-range laptop is unknown and unknowable from here. Raising `bodiesCeil` on an
operation count would trade a measured number for an unmeasured one - and it would be a difficulty
change wearing a performance coat, with `tools/endless-gauge.js` and the difficulty arc waiting to be
re-argued if it happened. The remainder is now its own PLAN item, and it is a reading and not a feature:
somebody with a browser and the F3 plate has to look at `draw ms` once.

### Things that bit, and are worth remembering
- **Relative millisecond claims do not survive a loaded box.** "A dying crowd steps *cheaper* than a
  standing one" (0.099 against 0.114 ms, and true every time on a quiet machine) failed once inside the
  40-way suite, where either number can be five times what it was. The test now says "no dearer to step"
  with a factor of two and says why in its comment. The rule this file now follows: **operations are
  exact and may be gated tight; milliseconds are orders of magnitude and may not.** That is why the step
  budget has 12x room over the game and the paint budgets have 18-21%.
- **The best-of-N trick only works on the thing you are timing.** Session 96's ladder takes the median of
  a batch for the same reason. The moment the same pass carries a second kind of number - what the scene
  was *holding* - the selection rule leaks into it. Sum what is order-independent; take the best of what
  is a wall clock; never both from one pass.
- **A measurement whose phase depends on the code path that precedes it will be re-litigated forever.**
  One extra `openScene` between the step and the paint is all it took to make the paint reading belong
  to the scene instead of to the run that came before it.
- **The F3 plate's worst step in a real run is 1.4-1.7 ms and it is not the crowd's fault.** That is
  fifteen times the steady 0.08-0.12 ms and it looked like a hitch worth chasing, so it was chased, for
  one scratch run: the record-setting frames do not line up with anything in the arena - deaths, wave
  arrivals, the boss, level-ups all had their own column and none of them were there - and one of them
  happened with **zero bodies on the glass**, where an empty arena steps in 0.004 ms. A pause from
  somewhere else, then: garbage collection, or a first-call warm-up, credited to the step because that
  is where the clock was standing. That is a different question from the one this session answered, and
  it is the first item below.
- **No release this session, on purpose.** Nothing a player can feel changed: the only `src/` edit is a
  comment in `balance.js`, and a release would have copied 0.10.6's files into a new folder and called it
  new. The tool and its tests are the deliverable; the next gameplay change releases.

### What should come next
1. **Find out what the 1.4-1.7 ms frames are, now that it is known they are not the crowd.** The question
   is per-frame *churn*, not growth: `tools/memory-hunt.js` proved the heap does not climb, so whatever
   those pauses are, it is short-lived. Two ways in, both cheap: run a probe scene under
   `node --trace-gc` and see whether the spikes are collections, and grep `src/game` for what a step
   allocates on purpose (`.sort(`, `.filter(`, `.map(`, array spreads, string building for labels and
   colours) - PLAN section 2 says "no allocation inside the per-frame loops" and nobody has ever checked
   that sentence with an instrument. If they are GC, the fix is a handful of reused arrays, not a rewrite;
   if they are not, the F3 plate's `worst` column is telling us something else and we should know what.
2. **Give the tool the other half of a real run: `--peak` in operations.** `peakOfRealRuns` already walks
   a real run frame by frame and reads the plate's milliseconds; handing the same hook through
   `makeFrameCost` would say what a real fight asks the canvas for (with the interface taken back out,
   as always) instead of only what a planted scene does. That is the number the art changes, and it is
   the number that would settle whether the two-second mean or the dearest frame is the right gate.
3. **The shot-speed line is still a weak card on every gun that can spend it** (session 97's item 1:
   1.009x / 0.979x / 0.988x on four seeds against 1.116x for pierce). Four seeds cannot tell 0.98 from
   1.02, so the first move is a re-measure with twelve or sixteen:
   `tools/line-ab.js --line bulletSpeed --weapon pulse --seeds 1-16`.
4. Still the two big ones: **the difficulty band**, which `tools/difficulty-arc.js` still fails, and the
   browser reading that is now PLAN's own item (one look at the F3 plate's `draw ms` on the owner's
   laptop, which is the only thing that can re-open `bodiesCeil`).
5. `tools/gun-tune.js`, still owed from session 96: patch one `BALANCE` row from the command line and
   play N seeds, as a real tool. `line-ab.js --set` is nearly enough for it now.

## Session 100 — Somebody else's ruler, the owner's song, and the release that carried both

Two things in one session, and only because the tree was dirty again: **`git status` showed session 99's
unfinished allocation work** (an untracked `tools/alloc-probe.js` of 600 lines, its test file, and the
two `src/` fixes it had found). Reading it and running it was cheaper than rewriting it for the third
time, so it got finished, verified and committed first. Then `OVERLORDS_REQUESTS` had a new line in it -
*"As soon as possible, use the file MenuMusic-SpaceRapBattle.flac as the main menu music and publish"* -
which is an order and not a milestone item, so it became the session's real work and it is **released as
v0.10.7**. Suite 1772 → **1803**; the reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session
98's both times it was asked, which it has to be: neither half of this touched the simulation.

### What landed, part one: what a step throws away (session 99's ruler, finished)
- **`tools/alloc-probe.js` weighs a step in garbage**, and the three things that make it honest are the
  deliverable: **one load per process** (a step that has only ever seen empty pools is compiled for empty
  pools, and the same 60 shots threw away 479 B a step as the first load a process saw and 3,145 B when
  an empty arena had been measured first), **the best of twelve 300-step windows**, and **every window
  the collector came into is thrown away and retried** - a window the collector interrupted reads *low*,
  so a plain best-of-N would keep the lies and call them the truth. It reads the heap twice
  (`heapUsed` and V8's new-space figure) and discards a window where they disagree, and it runs with a
  64 MB young generation so a window cannot fill it.
- **The reading answers session 97's question.** The F3 plate's worst steps of 1.4-1.7 ms are the
  collector, not the crowd: a scavenge of this heap measures 0.85-1.12 ms, and the crowd at its endless
  wall throws away a megabyte every 1.4 s of play (empty arena 184 B a step, the schedule's 100 bodies
  3.4 KB at 33 B a body, the wall of 200 6.1 KB, the same crowd dying 8.5 KB, PLAN's impossible scene
  19.6 KB).
- **The two fixes are in `src/`.** `core/grid.js`: a cell is `{ n, items }` now, because `cell.length = 0`
  throws the array's element store away and the next `push` buys a new one - and the hot door is
  `queryInto(x, y, r, out)`, which answers with a count and never touches `out.length` (a caller that
  cleared its scratch array put the allocation straight back). `game/awards.js` walks the ranks table
  once a step instead of `Object.keys` once per rule per step. **94 B a body a step down to 31 B.**
- **The rule is ratcheted, not met**, and PLAN says so in as many words: the budgets are 512 B an empty
  arena, 10 KB a gated load, 52 B a body - each about a quarter over what this commit measured, because
  a ratchet with no room in it gets raised the first time anybody needs it. The crowd still costs 31 B a
  body, and an ablation the previous session left in `.scratch` says where: of the schedule load's 3.9 KB
  a step, `updateEnemies` is 3.5 KB, `updateBullets` 1.2 KB, `updateAwards` 0.9 KB. That is next session's
  item and PLAN has it as one.
- Thirteen tests in `test/alloc-probe.test.mjs`, both gates mutation-checked, and `.scratch/` is gitignored
  from now on (throwaway measurements should not be what makes a tree dirty).

### What landed, part two: the menu's song (the overlord's request, shipped)
- `assets/MenuMusic-SpaceRapBattle.flac` - 8.7 MB, 80 s of 48 kHz stereo - is the attract screen's
  music. **`src/audio/track.js`** is the whole feature: fetch → `decodeAudioData` → a looping
  `AudioBufferSourceNode` on the **music bus**, so the music slider moves it, the master mute out-mutes
  it, and the player-hit muffle reaches it without this file knowing those exist. `patternFor` in
  `audio/music.js` asks `menuTrackIsUp()` and drops the generated title pad while it plays. Both ends
  glide on the track's own gain (in over a second - the sequencer keeps half a second of pad already
  scheduled, so a song that arrives over a second rises out from under the pad's tail instead of cutting
  across it; out over 0.3 s, because it is crossing under a run that has already begun).
- **The design is about not spending it.** Asked only when all three are true: an `AudioContext` exists,
  the visit is not muted, and the attract screen is the screen being looked at. Once, ever. The decoded
  samples are about 31 MB and the ordinary visit never pays either number, because the usual first press
  is the launch and the menu is gone by then. That is a test (`test/menu-track-cheap.test.mjs`), not a
  comment.
- **Which is the thing to know about hearing it**: no browser allows sound before a press, so a first
  visit is silent on the menu whatever the game does. The song is heard by anyone who unlocks audio
  without launching - `H`, `C`, `O`, `M` all call `initAudio` and all leave the title up - and after that
  it plays under the hangar, the codex, the settings, and whatever else they read. If the owner wants
  every visitor to hear it, the follow-up is a way back to the attract screen from the death's card
  (there is none today: the launch key is a new run). That is an interface decision and it is written in
  the archive entry as the honest limit, not as a defect.
- **Every failure is silent and written down**: `waiting / loading / ready / playing / missing / broken`,
  each with a `reason`, in `menuTrackLedger()` and `STARFALL.stats().menuTrack`. No network, no file, a
  browser with no FLAC decoder, a machine with no `decodeAudioData` at all - all of them leave the title
  playing the pad it played before, which is what the three extra test files prove.
- **The stub browser grew two things**: `network: { url: bytes }` (and no `network` means every request is
  refused, which is the shape of a missing file), and a `decodeAudioData` that refuses anything that does
  not begin with `fLaC`/`OggS`/`RIFF`/`ID3` and is absent entirely on `audio: 'raw'`. Both calling styles
  are honoured, because browsers have both.
- Sixteen tests in four files: `test/menu-track.test.mjs` (a visit that sits on the menu: asked once and
  once only, sequencer stood down, the run taking the bus back over a fade rather than a cut, and the
  song coming back on a *new* source via `resetToTitle` - a stopped source cannot be restarted), plus the
  cheap / missing / broken files above. `test/menu-track.test.mjs` also holds the two checks that keep a
  release from shipping silently songless: the file really is a FLAC, and `release.sh`'s copy list really
  names `assets` (it already did - the folder simply had never existed).

### Things that bit, and are worth remembering
- **A FLAC's declared length is in a 36-bit field and I read 24 of it.** The first parse said the owner's
  8.7 MB file was 0.31 s long; the STREAMINFO total-sample count runs from the low nibble of byte 21
  through four bytes, not three. The real answer is 3,839,488 samples at 48 kHz = 79.99 s, and every
  number in the docs above comes from that. Check a container header twice before quoting its numbers.
- **A rejected promise nobody watches can take a test process down.** `decodeAudioData` both takes
  callbacks and returns a promise; the track uses the callbacks and `.catch(() => {})` the promise, and
  `load(actx).catch(...)` has a net under it too - a song must not be able to take the frame loop with it.
- **"The menu is only seen before the first press" is not a bug you can fix from inside the page.** Every
  alternative (a media element, a gesture on mousemove, an autoplay ask) is either the same browser rule
  with more code or a rule the browser will enforce anyway. The honest move was to make the bytes cheap
  enough that the silent case costs nothing, and to say so plainly in the archive entry and the CHANGELOG.
- **A release is a good forcing function for "is it actually there".** `release.sh` copies `assets`
  (it had been in the list since before `assets/` existed), the test file asserts the list names it, and
  `releases/v0.10.7/assets/` is 8.7 MB as it should be. Old releases are untouched and still playable.
- No `git` history was rewritten; `git status` before anything else is now a habit with three saves to
  its name.

### What should come next
1. **The crowd's 31 bytes a body.** The rule in PLAN section 2 is ratcheted and not met, and the ablation
   has already named the three places: `updateEnemies` (3.5 KB of the schedule's 3.9 KB a step),
   `updateBullets` (1.2 KB), `updateAwards` (0.9 KB, still, after its table walk went). The method that
   finds them is ablation - copy the tree, switch one system's update off, weigh the step - and the trap
   is escape analysis: a line can allocate a lot cold and nothing at all warm, and only the warm number
   is paid for in a fight nine minutes old.
2. The shot-speed line is still a weak card on every gun that can spend it (session 97's item): re-measure
   with twelve or sixteen seeds before touching a number - `tools/line-ab.js --line bulletSpeed --weapon
   pulse --seeds 1-16`.
3. The difficulty band, which `tools/difficulty-arc.js` still fails, and the browser reading of the F3
   plate's `draw ms` that is the only thing that can re-open `bodiesCeil`.
4. `tools/gun-tune.js`, still owed from session 96.
5. If the owner wants the menu song heard by *every* visitor: a key back to the attract screen from the
   death's card. It is a real feature (the card already offers the hangar, the codex and the ship pick)
   and it is the only way the song reaches a visit that pressed Space first.

## Session 101 — The crowd's garbage was `Math.hypot`

Session 100's item one: *the crowd still throws away what it throws away*, 31 B a body against a 52 B
budget and an ablation that could only say "of a 3.9 KB step, `updateEnemies` is 3.5 KB". It was
`Math.hypot`, all the way down: **3.4 KB a step on the schedule crowd is now 816 B, the endless wall 6.1 KB
is 854 B, a body costs 3 B instead of 31**, and the budgets came down with the game (a load 10 KB to
2.5 KB, a body 52 B to 16 B). Suite 1803 to **1809**; released as **v0.10.8**.

### Why it was there
V8's `Math.hypot` takes any number of arguments, so it lays them out in a list on the heap and throws that
list away again on every call. The game called it **38 times over** - the stand-off band in `kinds.js`
(twice a step for every spitter and every shielder), the line a darter commits to, the flock's three pulls,
the bomber's circle, `blast`, `nova`, `missiles`, `turret`, `mines`, `tether`, `bosses`, the ship's own
input normaliser in `player.js`, and six places in the renderer. Every one of them two-argument.
`core/math.js` now exports a two-argument `hypot` - a multiply, an add, a square root - every call site
calls that one, and `test/structure.test.mjs` refuses `Math.hypot` anywhere else in `src/`, in the same
shape as the old `Math.random` guard. `test/math.test.mjs` is new and checks the swap is the same number:
it sweeps 4000 random lines across the arena and the worst relative disagreement with `Math.hypot` is
under 1e-12 (the helper's note says what it gives up - no overflow guard on the way in, which for a 3000 px
arena is four orders of magnitude away from mattering).

### What a byte is worth now, and what it means
Same tool, same box, same windows: `the schedule at full crowd 3,522 B to 816 B`, `endless at the body wall
6.1 KB to 854 B`, `the same crowd dying 8.5 KB to 1.2 KB`, `PLAN section 2's impossible scene 19.6 KB to
2.8 KB`. A browser's small young generation is now about **ten seconds of play** wide rather than a second
and a half, and since a scavenge of this heap costs a millisecond that is the F3 plate's 1.4-1.7 ms worst
steps, seven times rarer. Step *time* did not move (0.107 to 0.116 ms at the endless wall, i.e. the same
within the noise): this was never a speed win, it is a collector win.

### How it was found, and the two instruments worth keeping in mind
Both live in `.scratch` (gitignored) and are worth rebuilding rather than re-guessing:

1. **`sample-alloc.mjs` - V8's own allocation sampler, through `node:inspector`.** `HeapProfiler.startSampling`
   with `samplingInterval: 64`, `getSamplingProfile` after a few tens of thousands of steps, then walk the
   tree and total `selfSize` by `callFrame` and by caller-into-callee. It named the walks in `kinds.js` and
   then named `hypot @ ?:0` outright, which is what sent me looking there. **Its byte totals under-count by
   something like a hundred times** - a sample records the object that tripped the interval, not the bytes
   since the last one - so it is a naming instrument and never a ruler. `tools/alloc-probe.js` is the ruler.
2. **`ablate-parts.mjs` - ablation one level finer than a system.** Copy `src` + `tools` + `index.html` into
   `.scratch/abl`, replace one *part* of one function with nothing (the walk call, the separation loop, one
   argument list), and run the copy's own `alloc-probe.js --json` on the copy. That is how "updateEnemies is
   731 B of 816" became "the walk calls are 727 B of it" and then "the `glide` call inside `advance` is 334 B
   of that". `ablate-systems.mjs` is the same thing at whole-system grain; `mutation-check.mjs` is the third
   member and is the one that proves the gates still bite.

### Three traps, each of which wasted a measurement
- **Double boxing is not the story here.** The obvious theory for a few bytes a body was V8 storing a
  HeapNumber for every `enemy.x = <double>`. Measured on **the real enemies of a planted scene**, in a hot
  loop, one field at a time: `x`, `y`, `px`, `rot`, `timer`, `flash`, `hp`, `speed`, `ix`, `frost`, `spin`,
  `phase` - **0.0-0.1 B a write, every one of them.** Write a double into a plain object once and `%DebugPrint`
  it and you will see `@ Any`, which is what encouraged the theory; in optimised code it is not true. (Note
  that node 24 has no `%HasDoubleField` any more, so the field-representation question has to be answered by
  weighing writes, not by asking the map.)
- **A `for..of` over the crowd costs an iterator nobody can see**: 0.32 B a step for 200 bodies against 0.16 B
  for the indexed loop, i.e. nothing. Escape analysis eats it. I did not convert the loops.
- **An isolated copy of a hot function lies about its own cost.** Stepping 200 real enemies through one kind's
  `walk` in a standalone loop read **0.2-0.9 B a body**; the same walks inside the game are worth ~4 B a body
  between them, because in the game they are reached through one polymorphic `enemy.kind.walk` call site
  inside a step that is itself being optimised around everything else. Ablation inside the real scene is the
  only honest way in. Related: **ablation double-counts** - the system-level shares summed to 1081 B against
  an 816 B baseline, because switching one system off changes what the others do (`updatePlayer` came out at
  **-136 B**). Rank with it. Do not add it up.

### The ratchet, and why a ceiling has to move when the floor does
All three budgets were mutation-checked by putting the allocation back into a copy of the tree and running the
tool: `Math.hypot` back in the crowd reads **8.5 KB and fails**, a scratch object per `glide` reads **15 KB and
fails**, `cell.length = 0` back in `core/grid.js` reads **11.8 KB and fails**. Under the old 10 KB budget the
first of those three would have **passed** - the ceiling was the reason nobody had noticed. The test windows
also moved from `--steps 150 --windows 3` to `--steps 300 --windows 6`, because at 150 the empty arena alone
reads twice what it does at 300 and a budget set against a number that jangles with the window length is a
budget somebody raises out of irritation. FLOOR_BYTES stayed at 512 for the same reason.

### The reference run moved, on purpose
`--seed 20261006 --trace` is byte-identical to session 100's until frame ~11,280 and a different run after:
**10m00s / 73,982 / level 57 / 3,934 kills / 4,934 shards** (was 75,596 / 58 / 4,004 / 5,162). A rounding
error is enough to move a darter's aim by a hair, and a hair is enough. The four-seed batch moved +16% median
score, which is smaller than the gap between its own best and worst seed, so it is not a balance claim and no
number in `balance.js` was touched. Every tool that quotes a byte or a canvas-operation count still passes
unchanged: the perf probe's step and paint budgets were not touched by this, and `endless-gauge --check` is
unchanged for the same reason - `bodiesCeil` stays at 200 by session 99's decision.

### What should come next
1. **Nobody has weighed a painted frame.** `tools/perf-probe.js` counts canvas operations and `tools/alloc-probe.js`
   weighs the step; nothing in here weighs the garbage the *renderer* throws away at 60 fps, and the renderer had
   six of the 38 `Math.hypot` calls in it. The sampler says the paint path is close to clean now, but that is a
   name and not a budget. A `--paint` door on the alloc probe (the same window arithmetic, `renderFrame` instead
   of `stepWorld`) is the honest next instrument.
2. **What is left in the crowd is diffuse and probably not worth the price.** About 3-4 B a body, spread through
   the walks' arithmetic and the separation pass; the way to zero is positions and velocities in typed arrays,
   which is a rewrite of how the crowd is stored and not a sweep. Say so and leave it unless something else needs
   the storage change anyway.
3. Still open from before this session: the **shot-speed line** (`tools/line-ab.js --line bulletSpeed --weapon
   pulse --seeds 1-16`), the **difficulty band** that `tools/difficulty-arc.js` still fails, the **browser
   reading of the F3 plate** that is the only thing able to re-open `bodiesCeil`, and `tools/gun-tune.js` owed
   from session 96.
4. If another allocation hunt happens, start from the two instruments above rather than from grep. Two more
   variadic-builtin suspects were measured and are clean on this box: `Math.max(a, b, c)` and `Math.atan2` are
   free; `Math.hypot` is the odd one out.

## Session 102 — One arena a day: the daily run, seeded by the date

Milestone 10's next unchecked item: *a seed taken from the date, the same for everyone that day, with its
own best score*. It is **`src/game/daily.js` and one key, `T`**, and it is the whole of the feature - suite
1809 to **1837**, released as **v0.10.9**.

### What it is, in code
`todayDay()` reads the machine's date and returns it as a spoken number (`20261011`); `seedForDay(day)` in
`core/rng.js`'s new `seedFor` puts that number through the same `scramble` the mixer uses for successive
seeds, so consecutive days are unrelated arenas. `beginDailyRun(world)` writes `world.dailyDay` and the
day's seed into the world and `startRun` does the rest - a daily run is *not* a second mode, it is a run
launched from a different place. At the ending, `bankRun` (game/run.js) asks `bankDaily(world)`, which
compares the score against `bestOnDay(world.dailyDay)` and remembers `{ day, best }` in the save if the run
beat it. Four surfaces say it and all four say nothing for an ordinary run: `TODAY 4,321` as a fourth banked
number on the title, `TODAY 2026-10-11 · NEW BEST TODAY` on the card that ends a run, a `TODAY` row on the
pause rack beside `SEED`, and `TODAY 10-12` beside the HUD clock.

### The four decisions, and why
- **Local day, not UTC.** A shared UTC day is the more globally consistent answer and the less honest one:
  it calls yesterday's arena "today" for half the planet for a few hours and rolls a player's best over at
  four in the afternoon. Two people comparing scores are almost always in the same day already.
- **One day kept, not a history.** The save holds the latest day it saw and the best on it. Once today has
  begun, yesterday's best is a number nothing in the game can be compared against, and a stored field
  nobody reads is a field that quietly rots. `bestOnDay(day)` answers 0 for every other day, which is how a
  turned calendar says "nobody has flown today yet" without a single line of date arithmetic.
- **A daily banks everything an ordinary run banks** - all-time best, purse, codex, awards, log. A run that
  paid half as much for being on everybody's seed would be a punishment for taking the challenge. The day's
  best is an extra line on top.
- **`T` is a launch, not a mode.** One press flies today; the next `Space` flies a run of your own. Nothing
  is remembered about "being on the daily" except the day written into the run that was flown on it, so
  `Space` never changes meaning and there is no state to get stuck in.

### The bug, which was in `main.js` and nowhere else
The day's seed went into `world.seed` and stayed there, so the ordinary run after a daily one kept flying
the day. That field is load-bearing far beyond the game: it is how the address bar's `?seed=`,
`tools/simulate.js --seed`, the agent bridge and the test harness all hand a visit its arena, so three
existing tests failed loudly (`test/seed.test.mjs`, `test/history.test.mjs`, `test/agent-session.test.mjs`)
before anything was finished. The fix is a `visitSeed` in `main.js`: the seed an ordinary launch comes back
to, remembered on the way past the day's, and - the part that took a second thought - written only by the
run that first leaves the visit's own arena, or a second daily in a row would save the *day's* seed as the
ordinary one and the visit would never come back at all. `test/daily.test.mjs` pins the coming-back both
ways.

### Things worth remembering for the next session
1. **`new Date` is now banned in `src/game` except `daily.js`**, by a guard in `test/structure.test.mjs`.
   It is not pedantry: a run launched at 23:59 has to belong to the day it started on even if it is still
   flying after midnight, so the clock may be asked when a run is *launched* and never during a `step`. If a
   feature wants the date mid-step (waves that know it is Sunday), it passes the day in from the outside.
2. **A new DOM id has to be added to `tools/headless/harness.js`** or no test can see it; the harness throws
   on a missing id, which is the loud version of the mistake and worth having. `finalDaily`, `winDaily`,
   `titleToday` and `daily` in `stats()` are this session's additions.
3. **`remember()` is strict, `section()` is forgiving**, and that asymmetry is the whole save story: a bad
   value cannot be written (it throws, and `MAX_DAY = 99999999` is only enforced *there* - the day-equality
   check is what protects the read), and a bad value that arrives from an old or edited file reads as no
   value at all. `test/daily.test.mjs` checks both halves on purpose.
4. **No test freezes the clock.** Every daily test asks `todayDay()` and `seedForDay()` for its own numbers,
   so the suite passes whatever day it wakes up on. Freezing a date would have tested the arithmetic and not
   the contract, and the contract is "the day you are in".
5. **`Number.isSafeInteger`, not `Number.isInteger`,** for anything fed to the mixer - session 101's lesson,
   reused here: `1e21 >>> 0` is `0`, and a "whole number" that is too big to be one is how a seed silently
   becomes a constant.
6. **The title's control list is full.** It is not a style preference: index.html says the column is exactly
   as tall as the window it was designed for, and the type adds up to it. That is why the daily's key is
   written on the launch line (`... TO LAUNCH · T FOR TODAY'S ARENA`) instead of as a thirteenth row, and a
   test pins that sentence so nobody "tidies" the key out of the game.
7. **`tools/agent-bridge.js` grew `start { today: true }`** and `run_result` answers `daily`. The brief text
   in `agent-bridge.js` is what the model reads, so a new tool door has to be said there as well as
   implemented; `test/agent-session.test.mjs` checks the brief still describes what the game can do.
8. Ten mutations were run against the new tests (never bank, day-blind best, no seed coming back, month off
   by one, flag not cleared per run, card line not painted, HUD mark dropped, pause row dropped, `seedFor`
   made the identity, save ceiling widened, summary drops the day, a step asking the date) - **all caught**.
   Two of the first batch "survived" only because the sed could not express them; when a mutation script
   reports a survivor, check it actually applied before believing the gate is fine.

### What should come next
1. **Milestone 10 has one item left**: the browser half of the performance pass (line 1587), which this
   project cannot take by itself - it needs somebody with a real GPU and a devtools tab. Everything that can
   be measured headless has been measured and is under a budget.
2. Then **milestone 11**: a short first-run tutorial, the pass over every line of text in the game, and
   `1.0.0`. The daily's wording is the first thing a new player will now see that is not a control, so the
   text pass should look at `daily.js`'s four strings in the same breath as the title's.
3. Still open from earlier sessions: the **shot-speed line** (`tools/line-ab.js --line bulletSpeed --weapon
   pulse --seeds 1-16`), the **difficulty band** `tools/difficulty-arc.js` still fails, `tools/gun-tune.js`
   owed from session 96, and session 101's unfinished thought that **nothing weighs a painted frame** (a
   `--paint` door on `tools/alloc-probe.js`).
4. **One honest gap in the daily, left on purpose:** nothing compares your day against anybody else's,
   because there is no server and the save is local - "the same for everyone that day" is a promise about the
   *arena*, not about the scores. If that ever needs closing, the shape is a shareable line (day, seed,
   score) that a player can paste somewhere, and `tools/agent-bridge.js` is nearer to it than anything in
   the game is. Do not build a fake leaderboard.



## Session 103 — Three prompts that teach the hand. Released **0.10.10**

Milestone 10's next unchecked item: *a short first-run tutorial: three prompts that appear in play and
vanish once done*. It is **`src/game/tutorial.js` + `src/render/tutorial.js`**, three sentences on one
plate, and the whole of the design is in making them able to shut up. Suite **1837 → 1851**; the
reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session 101's (10m00s / 73,982 / level 57 /
3,934 kills / 4,934 shards, 7 vacuums, 2036 in), which is the proof a watcher watches.

### What landed
- **The three lines**: `W A S D TO FLY`, `MOUSE TO AIM · HOLD LEFT TO FIRE`, `SPACE TO DASH` - the three
  physical acts, in that order, one on the glass at a time. No fourth: **the cards already teach
  themselves** (`render/cards.js` prints `CHOOSE ONE · 1 2 3 OR CLICK` and puts a number chip in every
  corner, and a level-up that stops the run in front of three priced offers is the teaching), and the
  shard → XP → level loop is taught by its own bar filling under the ship.
- **A lesson is a latch, not a reading.** Each is checked every step - whether or not a plate was ever up
  for it - against something the run can be *seen* doing: 260 px of arena flown (the path walked, not
  the distance from the start, so out-and-back counts), a bullet in the air, `world.tally.dashes > 0`.
  The dash one borrows the tally's own definition, which is dashes *granted* and not fingers pressed, so
  the lesson means the same thing the ending's card means.
- **Each arrives at the moment it is about**: fly from the first step; fire when there is a body in the
  arena; dash when a body is inside `close` px **and the dash is ready**. `close` is 220 =
  `player.dash.distance`, so the hint lands at exactly the range one dash covers. The firing lesson has
  no distance at all, and that was a decision: the primaries' reaches run from the arc's 260 px to the
  pulse's 700, so any single number would be wrong for four of the five ships.
- **`BALANCE.tutorial`**: `runs` 3, `travel` 260 px, `close` 220 px, `hold` 9 s, `back` 6 s, `asks` 2,
  `arrive` 0.3 s, `away` 0.5 s. The last five are the unobtrusiveness budget - nine seconds on the
  glass, six before it will try again, **two attempts per lesson per run and then it is not put up
  again**, and a way out that takes half a second because a plate that is simply *gone* the instant you
  dash reads as a glitch and one that dims reads as "yes, that one".
- **The gate is the run log, not a flag**: lessons are offered while `world.pastRuns.length < 3`. A
  counter of its own ("has this save been shown the tutorial") would have taught every veteran whose save
  predates this file - twenty runs old, never shown anything - because their save has no such flag and
  the honest reading of "new" is the number of runs the document already holds.
- **The save keeps a set of lesson ids** (`tutorial.learned`, kind `names`: a lesson is learned once,
  there is no second rank of knowing how to dash), read once at boot into `world.tips` beside the purse
  and the codex and written at an ending like theirs - a mirror and never a cause, and never during a
  step. It is written as the game's whole set, so a document holding a name the game does not know is
  tidied rather than carried.
- **The place on the glass.** Bottom centre, above the XP bar's caption, because that is the one strip of
  this window nothing else ever asks for: score block top-left, hull top-right, boss bar and award plates
  top-centre, build rail down the left, XP bar at the very bottom. Cool edge (`cardEdge`), no gold -
  gold is what pays you and a lesson pays nothing - and refused outright over the cards, the pause rack
  and an ending, all three tested. `tutorialLayout(W, H)` is the `toastLayout` bargain again, so a test
  with no pixels can measure the plate and read the words that landed in it.
- **Fourteen tests in `test/tutorial.test.mjs`**, and the most important one is not about the plate at
  all: the same seed flown twice, once with all three lessons in front of it and once with nothing left
  to teach, **ends on the same `fingerprint`**. A module that reads the run must not be able to move it,
  and now there is an instrument that says so rather than a comment. Sixteen mutations were run against
  the file and all sixteen were caught (see below for the two that surprised me).
- Two existing files had to be told the truth, not patched around: `test/save.test.mjs`'s expected
  document and schema-order list now name the `tutorial` section, and `tools/headless/reset-audit.js`'s
  `OUTLIVES_A_RUN` grew **two** rows with a reason beside each - `tips`, and `prompt.teaching`, which is
  not itself kept but is the board's one reading of `tips` and so differs between two snapshots for a
  reason the run did not cause. `test/reset-state.test.mjs` caught this on the first run and it is a
  better test than the one I wrote: it sweeps the whole world for anything a run left behind.

### Decisions that will be asked about again
- **No settings row.** Nine rows is what fits the panel and a switch needs a tenth; more to the point,
  the prompts self-extinguish - three runs for a lesson nobody learns, and a save that has learned all
  three never sees one again. A hint that cannot outstay its welcome by more than three runs does not
  earn an off switch. If that is ever wrong, the switch is a row in `settingsIsUp`'s family and the whole
  mechanism hangs off `resetTutorial`'s `teaching`, which is one line.
- **Nothing tells the player the tutorial exists**: no title line, no codex row, no hangar note. A rule a
  player can never meet needs no disclaimer (the same call the deck filter made in session 97), and the
  only player these three lines can reach is one who has never seen the title screen's own control list,
  which is printed on the screen they arrive on.
- **The daily run is taught like any other run.** It is a launch and not a mode (session 102), and a
  daily flown at 00:05 by a visitor on their first visit is a first visit.
- `stats()` grew `tip` (the sentence on the plate, `''` when it is empty) and `tipsLearned`. A headless
  run cannot see the plate and "did the tutorial notice I can dash" was otherwise unaskable.

### Things that bit, and are worth remembering
- **`resetTutorial` must not ask whether a lesson's moment has come.** First version set `teaching` from
  `nextLesson(world) !== null`, and `nextLesson` asks `momentIsNow` - which at the instant a run is put
  together is *false for two of the three*, because the arena has just been emptied. Result: a save that
  already knew `fly` was never taught anything at all, silently. The gate asks whether a lesson is *left*,
  never whether its moment has arrived, and the comment says so, because "compute the state at setup from
  a predicate that is only true later" is a trap I would have set again.
- **A launch that clicks also fires.** `beginRun` spends the press so the launch is not also a dash, but
  firing is a *held* state and not an event, so a click-and-hold on the title has the ship firing on the
  first step and the gun's lesson is learned before it could be shown. That is the correct behaviour -
  they pressed the button - but it arrived as a surprise in a smoke test (`learned fire` at t=0.03) and
  the reason is worth writing down before somebody "fixes" it.
- **A timing test has to watch during the thing, not after it.** "Flying learns it, and the plate fades"
  first flew the ship for two seconds and *then* looked for the fade; the lesson was learned a second in
  and the fade was half a second, so the test found an empty glass and called it a cut. Same bug class as
