- **`carries` and `carriedBy` are both on every pair** on purpose: `carries` is what a test asserts and
  `carriedBy` is what the report prints. They are computed from the same two comparisons in one place.
- **The shape section is not a second promise.** Harm-vs-harm is still reported and not promised - the
  new rule only refuses a shared shape that *nothing* distinguishes, which is a weaker claim than
  "every body must be a step from every other" and the one that can actually be met by nine warm bodies.
- Milestone 9's `- [ ] Release.` was ticked rather than argued with. It is the fifth milestone to end
  this way and each of the others was ticked with the version that closed it; the work item before it
  (the colour-blind palette) shipped in 0.10.16 and the milestone's hotfix in 0.10.17.

### The orphan in the tree, part two
`tools/headless/harness.js` had an uncommitted `tapDash()` (press the right button wherever the pointer
already is, so a bot can dash without teleporting its aim), with a throwaway `.scratch/dash-probe.mjs` -
"which way does the bot dash, and what does it cost?" - that was its only caller. Nothing in `test/` or
`tools/` used it and no session wrote it down, so a previous run ended between the probe and its
conclusion. **Reverted** (it is dead weight in a tracked file; the helper is ten lines to put back) and
the probe is left in `.scratch` for whoever picks the dash question up. `test/afterimage-art.test.mjs`
does drive the dash through the mouse, but it aims on purpose, so it is not the consumer.

### What should come next
1. **Milestone 10**, which is what is left. The **difficulty band** (`tools/difficulty-arc.js` still
   fails), `tools/gun-tune.js` owed from session 96, session 101's **`--paint` door** on

2. The **dash question**, if the probe's owner wants it back: `--habit old`, `--range`, `--trigger` and

## Session 113 — The interface is measured: nine lines of type that could not be read can be now. Released **0.10.19**

Suite **1985 → 1998** (13 in `test/contrast.test.mjs`). The reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is
byte for byte session 112's again (10m00s / 73,982 / level 57 / 3,934 kills / 4,934 shards, 7 vacuums,
2036 in), which it must be: nothing in `game/` was touched, and every colour that moved is a colour the
simulation never reads.

Three sessions' notes ended with "the audit still has no opinion on the **interface**". It has one now, and
it was not a nice one: nine lines of the game's own type were written below the legibility bar, all of them
deliberately dim.

### The orphan in the tree, part three
`tools/contrast.js` (a whole measurement library, no CLI) and the three plate entries in
`core/palette.js` were sitting **uncommitted** at session start - session 112's owed item, written by a run
that ended before it could verify it. Nothing imported it, `test/contrast.test.mjs` did not exist, and the
plates it documented were only half-moved (session 113's own diff had `PALETTE.plate` in `hud.js` and the
`chipFace` swaps in `cards.js`, still uncommitted). Finishing it was the session: same shape as the palette
audit - `tools/contrast.js` is the ruler and the tables, `tools/contrast-check.js` prints them, and
`test/contrast.test.mjs` holds them - which meant splitting the file, because the draft had its report
running at import time and a test importing it would have run a report and called `process.exit`.

### What the ruler found, and what moved
Type gets **WCAG 2.1's contrast ratio** (4.5 to 1 for a line you read, 3 to 1 for a heading of `LARGE_PX`
24px or more) and not the Oklab step: a line of grey-on-navy type carries no hue and needs none, and
"can this be read" is a different question from "are these two bodies two". The Oklab step is printed
beside every number anyway so an interface figure can be compared with an arena one.

Failures, and where they ended up: `.entry.unknown .says` **2.43** → 4.73, `.award.unwon .says` **2.82** →
4.71, `.entry.unknown .name` **2.96** → 5.19, `.ship.locked .numbers` **3.22** → 4.88, `.setting .says`
**3.65** → 5.41, `.ship.locked` **4.12** → 5.35, `.award.unwon .name` **4.42** → 5.35, the mixer's quiet row
**3.05** → 4.82, the cold banish tab **3.31** → 6.43. Two more that merely cleared it thin came up too
(`.hull .says`, `.award .says`). The page's body blue went 6.46 → 7.05 and its numbers 5.03 → 5.60 so the
ladder stayed *stretched*: lifting the floor alone would have packed every rung into half a step.

- **A quiet line is paid for in colour and not in darkness.** The game dims a codex row it has not met, an
  award not yet won, a ship the purse has not bought, the slider nobody moved - and the honest signal for
  all of those is already something else: the glow (`text-shadow`), the gold price line, the dim key chip.
  So the rungs went greyer and stayed legible, and `test/contrast.test.mjs` refuses a quiet rung that
  carries more chroma than the rung above it, and one that is within 0.4 of a ratio of it. A "fix" that
  painted everything one bright flat wash would pass the bar and fail that.
- **The page half is read out of `index.html` itself** - every `color:` in its `<style>`, size resolved
  through the page's own inheritance (`.entry.unknown .name` asks `.entry.unknown`, then `.entry`, and
  takes the smallest `clamp()` branch when there is one), dimmed by the rule's own `opacity`, composited
  over a veil parsed from the same file. `pageColourRules()` is the same parse with the audited rows taken
  back out, and a test asserts the counts match, so a new selector cannot be filtered into silence.
- **The glass half is a table pinned to the drawing twice.** Every colour by `core/palette.js` name, and a
  test reads the function that paints each pinned line and refuses a name it never mentions, plus one that
  paints the mixer for real and reads the ink, the alpha *and* the point size back off the canvas stub.
  That pin is what caught the draft's own error: the banish tab was being measured in `cardEdge` while
  `drawBanishTab` had long since moved its hot ink to `playerLine`.
- **The three plates are palette entries** (`plate`, `plateDeep`, `chipFace`) and a test greps `src/render/`
  for their literal `rgba(` spellings, because a plate copied into a draw call is a plate that stops being
  true. A translucent colour is composited before it is measured, everywhere, same rule `sights.js` uses.
- **`tools/sights.js`'s "if and when somebody wants it"** pointer to `tools/contrast-check.js` was left
  four sessions ago in a comment that anticipated exactly this file. It now points at a tool that exists.

### The mistake that cost the most, and it was avoidable
**I destroyed work with `git checkout -- <file>`.** To falsify the new guards I mutated a colour, ran the
test, and "restored" with `git checkout`. Half the files I mutated carried **uncommitted** work - mine and
session 113's - and `git checkout` handed back HEAD: four files lost the plate extraction, the tab ink,
`ROW_QUIET` and every CSS colour lift in one line. I rebuilt all of it from the diff printed at the top of
this session, and the suite is green again, but only because I had read that diff. **Rules for the next
session: copy the file to `/tmp` and copy it back (that is what the mutation runs in this note should have
been), and treat `git checkout --` as a destroyed-work machine whenever the tree is dirty.** A dirty tree is
normal here - an orphan session left one at the start of this one, and it will again.

Every guard was then falsified properly, with backups: a dimmed codex line, `ROW_QUIET` back to 0.5, the tab
ink back to `cardEdge`, an inline plate in `hud.js`, a locked row as bright as an owned one, a new dim
selector, a mixer row lying about its size - each turned exactly the named test red and nothing else did.

### Decisions, so nobody relitigates them
- **Four exclusions, each one written down in the tool**: a `text-shadow` is not counted (a line that only
  reads because of its glow should be shouted about, not passed); a pulsing line is measured at full
  strength, like a bomber's flash; `.screen.aside` is not a legibility question (session 111's tenth is on
  purpose) - and a test notes that the two exclusions currently carry no colours at all, so a colour put
  there is reported rather than skipped; and the developer's readouts (the F3 plate, the frame-rate line)
  are exempt on `test/words.test.mjs`'s grounds.
- **Every page line is measured on the *brightest* field**, because the four veils are all nearly black and
  light-on-dark type is worst on the brightest. A test holds them within an order of magnitude of each
  other and under luminance 0.05, so the day a panel gets a real background the audit is forced to grow a
  per-panel field instead of lying.
- **The report prints `thin` lines on a clean run** (five today: 4.71-4.88), the way `palette-check.js`
  prints the pairs near their bar. A clean run should say where the edge is.
- The harness's text log gained `ink` and `alpha` (session 111 did the same for strokes). Anything that can
  measure a *painting* should, over a remembered table - that is the third time that sentence has been
  true in this project.

### What should come next
1. **Milestone 10's remaining work**: the **difficulty band** (`tools/difficulty-arc.js` still fails),
   `tools/gun-tune.js` owed from session 96, session 101's **`--paint` door** on `tools/alloc-probe.js`,
   then the browser half of the performance pass - and `1.0.0`.
2. Small things this session saw and left: `.setting .says` is now brighter than the base hangar row and
   that is fine but accidental, and the two mixers (the readout and the settings rack) still describe their
   quiet states in two different ways - an alpha in one and a colour in the other; `cageWall` is still a
   thin wall for a protanope (deliberately unjudged); and the crowd pair `darter`/`swarmling` still wants a
   silhouette, which remains an art job for a session with eyes on a screen.
3. If a third ruler ever wants the same shape (text on the *arena* background, e.g. a floating score label
   over a bright nebula), `contrast.js` already composites over an arbitrary field - but `nebula.js` bakes
   its own pixels and the audit declines to invent a brightness for a sprite, so say what the field is first.

## Session 114 — The bot's dash is a get-out now, and pressed a tenth as often

**No release, on purpose.** Everything this session changed lives in `tools/`; the only `src/` edits are
comments in `balance.js`. The game a player opens is the one 0.10.19 shipped, byte for byte - the
reference run is identical - and a version in the owner's menu that nobody can tell from the one under it
is noise, not progress. The next session that moves the game itself releases, and it will have two
balance rows' worth of fresh measurement to say for itself.

Suite **1998 → 2012** (14 in `test/dash-habit.test.mjs`). The reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is
byte for byte session 113's again (10m00s / 73,982 / level 57 / 3,934 kills / 4,934 shards, 7 vacuums,
2036 in), which is the point of `--dash` existing: nothing about the shipped bot moved, and every number
in this file that was measured without it still means what it said.

The item was PLAN's "the bot's dash habit is a dive in and not a get-out". It was two bugs wearing one
coat, and the second was the expensive one.

### What was wrong, and what it cost
`dashEscape` pressed the dash *at* the nearest body by moving the pointer there and clicking the right
button. Two things follow from that. The dash goes where the movement keys point if any are held and the
pointer only if none are (`src/game/player.js` `dashDirection`), so half the time it was not even a dive -
it was wherever the policy's flee was already taking it - and the pointer move took the guns off whatever
they were aimed at, which is the one thing the bot's aim has to keep. And it pressed whenever anything came
within 170 px, a number borrowed from the walk's own panic distance, which in a crowd is every cooldown
forever: 58 to 164 dashes a run depending on the build.

Sixteen careless seeds, ten minutes each, and the same seeds with the habit switched off as the floor:

| habit, at 170 px | aware+random middle / died / score | human+random middle / score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| never presses | 4m23s / 9 of 16 / 12,914 | 2m33s / 3,173 |
| the dive, as shipped | 1m07s / 10 of 16 / 5,754 | 1m13s / 1,799 |
| the get-out, as shipped | 5m11s / 12 of 16 / 5,773 | 2m27s / 2,316 |

Every habit that pressed was *losing runs*. The instrument was costing the thing it measured.

### Which way, and when
The new habit is `escape`: press only when a body is actually within reach, throw the ship the way the
crowd is *not* (every body within `push` px pushing on it, nearest loudest), give any wall the veto over
the axis it stands on - and if that leaves nothing, keep the press instead of spending it on a wall. The
press is `game.tapDash()`, the right button down and up on the spot the pointer already stood, so the aim
is not moved at all. `DASH_HABITS` is `off, escape, dive, along` and `--dash-habit <name>` picks one
through `tools/simulate.js`, `tools/line-ab.js`; `tools/dash-habit.js` is the ladder that ranks them and
exits non-zero under `--strict` when the shipped one is not the one to ship.

Sweeping `--trigger` over 30, 45, 60, 90, 110, 170 px turned out to be the finding, not the direction:

| trigger | aware+random middle / died / score / dashes a run | human+random middle / score / dashes a run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| never presses | 4m23s / 9 of 16 / 12,914 / - | 2m33s / 3,173 / - |
| 170 px | 5m11s / 12 of 16 / 5,773 / 107 | 2m27s / 2,316 / 58 |
| 90 px | 5m17s / 8 of 16 / 9,790 / 39 | 2m54s / 3,347 / 30 |
| 60 px | 4m16s / 3 of 16 / 49,593 / 17 | 3m05s / 5,537 / 23 |
| **45 px** | **7m20s / 1 of 16 / 42,893 / 12** | **4m32s / 5,998 / 16** |
| 30 px | 5m13s / 3 of 16 / 24,158 / 6 | 4m00s / 4,115 / 10 |

45 px is one body-reach - contact plus the dozen pixels a closing body covers between two of a person's
looks - and it is what ships, in `DASH` next to the habit. On the careful build (aware, wise picks, twelve
seeds at a quarter hour) nothing dies either way and the habit costs nothing: score medians 117,007 against
the floor's 117,814, at 7.8 presses a run instead of 164.

### Things that surprised me
- **The verdict had to be bought with the score, not the deaths.** The first version of `tools/dash-habit.js`
  ranked on the middle of the deaths, and at the loose trigger that said the get-out habit was fine (5m11s
  against a 4m23s floor) while those runs were making *half* the score of a bot that never presses. A
  habit that spends every cooldown running survives a bit longer and plays worse. The check is now
  two-sided - nothing that dashes may beat the shipped habit by 10%, and the shipped habit may not fall 10%
  *under* the never-presses floor - and `--trigger 170 --strict` fails it, which is the falsification that
  says the check has teeth. `--strict` on the shipped defaults passes.
- **`dive` does not really dive, and the column said so.** `at a body` reads 70-76% for the dive habit at
  170 px and 13-21% at 45 px, because at a reach the policy always has a flee key held and the keys beat
  the pointer. So most of the old habit's harm was the pointer yank and the hundred wasted presses, not the
  heading; held at 45 px the dive middles 4m28s against the get-out's 4m32s and the ladder cannot tell them
  apart at all. Direction and timing are both fixed because a habit is one thing, but only one of them was
  worth three minutes of a run.
- **The tether's whole measured worth was the bot's dash rate.** With the old habit a cord stood for 54,452
  of a run's 108,000 steps - half the run. With the new one `tools/line-ab.js --line tether --dash` reads
  482 of 54,000 steps at five free ranks and 1,566 at three dealt, and five free ranks are worth +1.5%
  score and nothing to the damage column, against the +2..5.3% the row was priced off. `tether.damage` is
  left where it is on purpose: the rate the card is bought at is a player spending dashes on the knot,
  which is nearer the old instrument than the new one, and re-tuning a row because the bot forgot to use it
  is how a balance table eats itself. Written up as a new "After 1.0" item instead. `afterimage`'s deck
  numbers were re-read the same way (0.946x dealt, 0.997x free - the card still does nothing measurable,
  and now on a batch where the out line is not dying at 4m51s, so the ratio means something).
- **A careful batch is not a verdict.** `off,escape,dive,along` on aware+wise at 900 s: nothing dies, so
  there is no middle of any deaths to compare, and a PASS there would be a claim about a window that
  measured nothing. The tool says `NOTHING RANKED` and exits non-zero, and its defaults are the *careless*
  build for the same reason `tools/difficulty-arc.js`'s are.
- **`tapDash` refuses to invent a place to press.** The harness remembers where the pointer was last put and
  throws if nothing ever put it anywhere, because pressing at (0, 0) would be pressing at a corner of the
  window and not nowhere. Small thing; it is the difference between a dash that aims and a dash that guesses.

### What is next
Re-price the dash lines against an instrument that presses the way a buyer of them would (PLAN's new item):
`tether.damage`, `afterimage.bait` - whose 6%/30% crowd-attention figures were read with the dive habit and
probably read *low*, since a get-out leaves its images behind a fleeing ship, which is exactly where a
chasing crowd is - and what `overcharge` is worth now that the bot's dash is not spent on nothing.

## Session 115 — The allocation ruler was weighing its own compiler. All three budgets came down

**No release, on purpose.** Everything is in `tools/` and `test/`; not one byte of `src/` moved, so the game
in the owner's menu is 0.10.19's. What this session buys is that the performance pass can be finished at
all: the gate that is supposed to say "a step throws away less than it used to" had been sitting at FAIL
for a whole milestone, and every number in `PLAN` and in this file that came out of it was inflated by
however much V8 happened to be compiling that day.

Suite **2012 → 2014** (two new in `test/alloc-probe.test.mjs`, which is now 14 tests and 1m14s of the
suite's 2m11s). `node tools/simulate.js` still plays a whole game. The mutation guard still bites: putting
`Math.hypot` back into `core/math.js` reads the endless wall at **5.3 KB** a step against a 1,280 B budget,
so the tighter budgets have more teeth than the loose ones, not less.

### The bug, and why it hid for a milestone
`WARM_STEPS = 2400` steps in one synchronous `for` loop, then measure. That is not warm. Measured directly:
20,000 uninterrupted steps of the endless wall left the first reading at **2,660 B** a step, and the same
crowd stepped with the event loop handed back every 60 steps settled at **606 B** and stayed there from its
first window. V8 installs the code it compiles in the background when the loop turns, so a warm-up that
never turns weighs whatever the load started on. A browser turns the loop every frame, which is the whole
argument for measuring the warm number; the cold number was a ruler measuring itself.

That is why `the ratchet` failed under `node --test` and passed on its own: the reading depended on how much
stepping the process happened to do, and a loaded box does fewer turns.

What a load actually costs, warmed, reproducible to under a percent across a dozen runs and unchanged by six
CPU burners (they were read *identical* under load, which is the proof the fix is real):

| load | cold, as the file had it | warm, now | budget, now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the arena on its own | 184-415 B | **64 B** | 128 B (was 512) |
| the schedule at full crowd | 1.1 KB | **436 B**, 4 B a body | 1,280 B (was 2,560) |
| endless at the body wall | 1.4 KB | **574 B**, 3 B a body | |
| the same crowd, dying | 1.8 KB | **984 B**, 5 B a body | |
| the same crowd, spread out | 1.6 KB | **582 B**, 3 B a body | |
| 900 sparks alone / 60 shots alone | 184-219 B | **64 B / 65 B** - nothing over an empty arena | |
| PLAN section 2's impossible scene | 19.6 KB | **3.8-4.1 KB**, 6-7 B a body | not gated |

The warm-up is now `warmWork`: measure the load in windows of its own - 1,000 steps, forced collections, the
same two readings an ordinary window takes - until **six in a row land within 10% of each other**. A *band*
of probes and not "this one was near the best", because the readings bounce on the way down (the wall dips
to 831, rises to 1,080, settles near 580) and a rule that stops on a lucky dip stops twice as high as the
truth: at 12,000 steps the empty arena sometimes plateaus at 184 B and never falls to its real 64. A load
that is still getting cheaper at `WARM_MAX_STEPS` reports `warmSettled: false` and **fails the gate**, so a
broken ruler cannot be read as a pass. Cost: a load wants 20,000-47,000 steps of warm and a full ladder is
about a minute. `WARM_PROBE_STEPS` is not a free knob - at 2,000 the same crowd reads a fifth cheaper again
- and the budgets above are set against 1,000.

### The second bug, which the first one was hiding
With the warm-up fixed, `--windows 6` and `--windows 24` still disagreed, and in the *wrong* direction: the
wall read 574 B at six windows and **189 B** at twenty-four. Dumping every window (`.scratch/alloc-dump.js`
is a copy of the tool with the window list printed - that is what `.scratch/` is for) showed why. The
readings sit in a tight cluster, 567-610 B, and about **one window in a hundred reads half the truth**: the
one that was caught had grown 59 KB off `heapUsed` and **176 KB** off the young generation, and reported
197 B a step. Old space hands a page back inside a window and `perf_hooks` never calls that a collection, so
the delta reads low - and a best-of-N rule is a magnet for exactly those windows, the more windows the more
likely one turns up.

The file's header has claimed since it was written that it "reads the heap twice and throws away a window
where they disagree". Nothing ever compared them. Now `readingsAgree` does, a fifth of the larger reading or
4 KB, and the liar is refused like any other bad window. Both new tests exist because of this: that six and
twenty-four windows agree, and that a window whose two readings disagree is not a reading.

### Worth knowing before the next perf item
- **The dearest gated load is no longer the wall, it is the crowd dying: 984 B a step, 5 B a body, against
  574 B for the same crowd alive.** The 410 B a step that killing and replacing 200 bodies costs is about
  as much again as the same 200 bodies walking. That is where the next cut in `src/` belongs and it is the
  only load within 30% of a budget.
- A megabyte of garbage is 8.9 s of play at the dying crowd and 15 s at the living wall, and a scavenge of
  this heap measures 0.85-1.12 ms - so the dying crowd is where the F3 plate's worst frames come from.
- `measureLiveRun` (the `--live` and `--run` rows) is still played **cold**, and its comment and its own
  printed line both say so: a stretch is one synchronous run of frames with no turn of the event loop in
  it, and so is the single 30-second run played beforehand to set the scene, so the row carries its own
  warm-up inside it - **4.7 KB a step** against the warmed loads' 570-980 B, which is a ceiling and not a
  cost. Warming it properly means playing two or three more of those 30-second runs with a turn of the
  event loop between them (~10 s of the box each, and the flag costs about half a minute of the report as
  it is) before the measured stretch, so it is left. If a future session wants that row to mean what the
  planted rows mean, that is the fix: `playOneRun` twice more with a `setImmediate` between the plays,
  then plant and measure as now.
- Budgets are set about a third over the dearest warm reading, not on a rounding error. If a future session
  wants them tighter, widen `WARM_PROBE_STEPS` first and re-set them from what the wider probe says.
- `node --test` is 2m11s and `test/alloc-probe.test.mjs` is over half of it. That is the price of a byte
  count that means something; do not "fix" it by shrinking the warm-up, which is where the flakiness was.

### What is next
First, the new item this session wrote into PLAN's milestone 10: **cut what the crowd costs when it is
 dying** (984 B a step against the living wall's 574 B), which is the one place `src/` has an allocation
 problem with a number attached to it and no fix yet.
Then the three open items of milestone 10, unchanged and with the first of them unblocked by this session:
**the browser half of the performance pass** (open the game, read the F3 plate, compare against the
574-984 B a step the ruler now says is the truth), then **Release 1.0.0**. The After-1.0
re-price of `tether`/`afterimage`/`overcharge` is still sitting there from session 114 and is still the
lowest-stakes of the lot.

## Session 116 — The dearest thing in a crowded step was the sound it asks for. Released 0.10.20

**Released v0.10.20.** This one moves `src/`, and it is the sort of change the owner's menu should carry: the
game looks identical and sounds identical, and the worst frames in a fight are the collector, which it now
interrupts a quarter less often. Suite **2014 → 2023** (9 in `test/cues.test.mjs`). The reference run
(`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session 115's (10m00s / 73,982 / level 57 / 3,934 kills /
4,934 shards, 7 vacuums, 2036 in) — a cue never feeds back into a run, and 4,968 of them in a two-minute
fight make sure of it.

The item was PLAN's "cut what the crowd costs when it is dying". It was not the dying. **It was the sound
queue**: `cueBeep`/`cueNoise` pushed a fresh object per sound, and a crowded step asks for 1.7 sounds — a
darter's beat, two shots landing, a death, the shards it paid out. That one `queue.push` was **295 B of the
410 B** separating the crowd dying (984 B a step) from the same 200 bodies standing still (574 B), and it
was the last big single allocator left after `Math.hypot`.

### How the bytes were attributed, since the ruler cannot name a cause
`tools/alloc-probe.js` weighs a step; it has no idea which system spent it. So, exactly as the `Math.hypot`
hunt did it: **`git worktree add /tmp/wt HEAD`, switch one suspect off in the copy, weigh the same load
again** (~7 s a weighing once you know what you want). And `node --heap-prof --heap-prof-interval=1024` with
`.scratch/read-heap2.mjs` (prints full stacks over a size floor) for names. What that bought:

| switched off | the crowd dying reads |
| --- | --- |
| nothing (as it was) | 984 B a step |
| the cue objects | **689 B** |
| the whole shard drop-and-pickup path | 533 B |
| both | 393 B |
| the `'+' + enemy.score` label string | 980 B |

The two big rows overlap by ~155 B (the pickup pings are cues), which is why the ablations are read as a
lattice and not added up. The last row is the lesson: a string concatenation per kill is worth **4 B a
step**, because V8 does not allocate what it can see the whole life of. It was measured, written down, and
left exactly where it was — the third time this project has saved a session by refusing to fix a plausible
guess.

### What shipped
`game/cues.js` is a `core/pool.js` pool now. One record shape for all four kinds (one hidden class instead
of four), every queue function writes every field — the contract every other pooled list in the game keeps —
and **a drained cue is on loan**: `drainCues(handle)` hands the whole frame's batch over and returns every
record when `handle` returns, inside a `finally`. `audio/sfx.js` had to work that way anyway (it cannot
spend its voice budget until it has seen the frame), so its mix now sorts and plays *inside* the drain.
`copyCue(cue)` is how a listener keeps one; 12 test listeners went through the new `tools/headless/hear.js`
instead of hand-rolling the copy.

Two decisions worth keeping:
- **The batch and not the cue.** A per-cue callback would have failed *silently* if a call site had been
  missed — a batch read as a cue has no `kind`, so audio would have played nothing and no test would have
  noticed. `grep -rn "drainCues("` is the guard, and `hear()` is the one place the shape is written.
- **`drainCues` returns the records in a `finally`,** so a listener that throws mid-frame cannot leave the
  queue stuck full replaying itself forever. Falsified by copying the file to `/tmp`, dropping the
  `finally`, and watching `test/cues.test.mjs` go red — and *not* with `git checkout --`, per session 113.

The numbers: schedule crowd **436 → 407 B**, endless wall **574 → 514**, crowd dying **984 → 735**, spread
out **582 → 499**, PLAN section 2's impossible scene 3.9 → **3.3 KB**. A megabyte of garbage is 11.9 s of
the dearest load instead of 8.9 s. `STEP_BYTES` 1,280 → **896** and `BODY_BYTES` 8 → **5**, and for the
first time the tightened gate was pointed at the regression that paid for it: `git worktree add /tmp/wt2`,
put an object per sound back, and the dying crowd reads **984 B and FAILS (exit 1)**. Every earlier budget
in this file was mutation-checked against an allocation that had already been deleted and could only be
re-invented; this one could simply be put back, and was.

### Things that surprised me
- **A pooled queue is not a queue that does nothing.** The ablation said 689 B; the pool says 735 B. The 46 B
  a step between them is `spawn`/`clear` bookkeeping and eleven field writes per sound, and it is the honest
  price of keeping the fight audible rather than silently not making the sound. Said out loud in the module
  header so nobody reads the ablation number as the achievable one.
- **An instrument that skips the frame loop reads its own omission.** My `.scratch/dying-profile.mjs` stepped
  the world without draining cues (the real frame does, `main.js` → `consumeCues`), so the first profile
  *after* the fix still showed megabytes under `makeCue` — the pool growing because nothing was handing the
  records back. Adding the drain made the picture honest again, and then nothing in `src/` scored over
  200 KB across a whole fight. Same family as session 114's instrument-that-measured-itself; the rule is
  "a probe must empty the queue exactly as a frame does", which `tools/alloc-probe.js` already knew and I
  did not.
- **`test/structure.test.mjs`'s `Math.hypot` guard is a text grep over all of `src/`,** so writing the words
  `Math.hypot` in a *comment* in `cues.js` failed the suite. That is the guard being literal rather than
  clever — the fix was to name the thing differently in prose ("the crowd's distances went through
  `core/math.js`'s own `hypot`"), and it is worth knowing before you write about it in a comment anywhere
  else in `src/`.
- **One `node --test` run reported `fail 2` and the next `fail 1`.** The extra one did not reproduce and was
  in `test/alloc-probe.test.mjs`, which is the suite's flakiest file because it spawns probing children
  while eight other files are probing too. Nothing was changed for it; if the suite goes red there without a
  change to `src/`, look at load before you look at the code. The tightened budgets still have room — the
  dearest load is 22% under `STEP_BYTES` — but that is the margin to watch.

### What is next
The two open items of milestone 10, in order: **the browser half of the performance pass** (open the game,
F3 plate, fly the endless door to `bodies 200 / 200`, and write down what `step ms` and `draw ms` say — the
ruler now says 514-735 B a step and 0.11 ms a step is what the arena knows; only a real canvas can say what
a real machine asks), then **Release 1.0.0**.

And the dead end, written down so nobody re-walks it: after the queue, the sampler names no site in `src/`
worth cutting. The crowd dying still costs ~221 B a step more than the same crowd standing, and that residue
is diffuse — the grid hunt already said the same about the walk. Typed-array positions for the crowd or
nothing. The After-1.0 re-price of `tether`/`afterimage`/`overcharge` from session 114 is still sitting
there, still the lowest-stakes of the lot.

## Session 117 — The three dash lines were re-read against the dash that ships. No number moved, and two of them can be measured again

Suite **2023 → 2043** (19 in `test/ghost-grid.test.mjs`, 1 new in `test/overcharge.test.mjs`). The
reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session 116's again (10m00s / 73,982 /
level 57 / 3,934 kills / 4,934 shards, 7 vacuums, 2036 in) - the only `src/` numbers added are two
counters that feed nothing back into a run, which is what makes that sentence testable rather than
hopeful.

**No release, on purpose.** The counters are invisible: the game in the owner's menu behaves and looks
and sounds exactly as 0.10.20's does, and a version nobody can tell from the one under it is noise
(sessions 114 and 115 held the same line for the same reason). The next session should ship
**1.0.0**, which is the only milestone-10 item left that this project can do by itself - see the last
section.

The item was PLAN's "re-price the two dash lines against the habit that ships now" (After 1.0, owed
from session 114). Three numbers were in its scope: `tether.weight`, `afterimage.bait`, and what
`overcharge` is worth now the bot's dash is a get-out. All three were read; **none moved**, and each
one now has a reason with a number behind it instead of a paragraph of hope.

### What was wrong with the old readings, in one line each
- **`afterimage.bait` 110 px** was chosen by session 42 off a grid read with the *dive* habit at a
  170 px trigger - a bot that pressed the dash twenty times a minute and threw itself at what
  frightened it. Session 114 replaced that habit with one that presses ~ten times a *quarter-hour*
  and leaves its images behind a fleeing ship. Both halves of the instrument moved under the number.
- **`tether.weight` 5** was defended in the row by "a thread is worth about a mine's blast per body
  and happened a quarter as often" - and the quarter was the old habit's rate, which session 114
  measured as nearer a twentieth.
- **`overcharge`** had never been measured on a dashing instrument at all: its deck A/B in the row was
  read on a bot that never pressed the dash, and its "6.3 loaded pulls a minute" came from a
  throwaway script that no longer exists.

### What shipped
- **`tools/ghost-grid.js`** - the ruler session 42 had to write as a throwaway, made permanent and
  made a check. It plays a grid of (radius × rank) cells on the same seeds, pins the rank after every
  step, sets `BALANCE.upgrades.afterimage.bait` live (the sim reads it per call, so the sim itself is
  never touched), and samples every frame a ghost is standing: how many bodies are within 250 px of
  the ship and how many of them `quarryFor` answers with a ghost. Two denominators are printed,
  because a rooted body - a sniper, a place in the Hive's wall - cannot be diverted by anything and
  has no business in the denominator of a share of what got diverted; the "every body in the ring"
  figure is kept beside it so session 42's grid is still readable. It carries session 42's three
  promises as checks (`--strict`): a first rank felt (`FLOOR` 4%), a fifth under the ceiling
  (`CEILING` 40% - past it the crowd stops coming and the fight ends by itself), and a slope of at
  least twice (`SLOPE`), which is the test that refused 150 px back then.
- **The overcharge line keeps two counters now** - `overchargeLoaded` (steps the gun stood full) and
  `overchargeSpent` (pulls that went out loaded), on `game/overcharge.js`'s record and on `stats()`,
  so `tools/line-ab.js --line overcharge --stats overchargeLoaded,overchargeSpent` prints the rate
  the row has always quoted from a lab. A fresh/cold gun counts 0 in both, a run without the card
  counts 0 in both, and `resetRun` takes them with the charge - all four are tested, and one real
  flown run reads them through `stats()`.
- Every number quoted below is also written into the three balance rows, dated, with the command that
  reproduces it.

### The measurements
`afterimage`, ten seeds of five minutes, the shipped get-out habit, ranks pinned:

| bait | rank 1 | rank 3 | rank 5 | slope 1→5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 72 px | 7.7% | 19.3% | 19.0% | 2.47x |
| 90 px | 15.9% | 21.4% | 30.2% | 1.90x |
| **110 px (ships)** | **16.5%** | **35.7%** | **37.0%** | **2.25x** |
| 130 px | 19.9% | 45.2% | 51.1% | 2.57x, over the ceiling |

Session 114's prediction held: the images a get-out leaves behind a fleeing ship stand in the road the
crowd is walking down, and the share turned aside went from 6.4%/30.2% to 16.5%/37.0% at the two ends
of the ladder. **`bait` stays at 110 anyway.** The radius sweep says it is the best-shaped of the four
(130 px is over the ceiling - that is the crowd stopping coming; 72 and 90 buy a *flatter* ladder,
which falsifies the idea I went in with, that a narrower disc would buy back the slope), and the
verdict on the shipped radius clears all three promises on a batch with a real sample.

`tether`, eight seeds at the cap, the shipped habit, read per event this time with the counters
`game/tether.js` has kept since its first session: three ranks the bot bought for itself tied a fan 6
times, pulsed 22, came round 37 bodies - **1.68 bodies a pulse**, **0.56 of a body standing on the
threads** over a live step; five free ranks tied 2, pulsed 6, came round 6.5 (1.08, and 0.18) because
a ship with all five is hardly ever cornered. At those runs' damage rank a pulse is 5 × 2.2 = 11 hull
a body, so the line paid **0.7%** of the dealt batch's damage and **0.1%** of the free one, where the
old instrument reported ~6%. **`weight` stays at 5**: 1.08-1.68 bodies a pulse against a mine's 1.11 a
blast is the same near crowd whoever sweeps it (session 45's finding, repeated), and there is no press
rate a person has at which 5 is too strong - at the panic rate it bought +2.1..5.3% of a run's score,
at the get-out rate it is invisible. A card that is never too much and often nothing is priced on a
wager on the player, which is what the row always said. What the batch *does* say is the `dealt`
column: 0.972x - three levels spent on the line cost a run 2.8% of its score, so an instrument that
buys it and cannot use it pays twice.

`overcharge`, eight seeds at the cap, five free ranks: **+3.4% of the damage column** on the get-out
habit against **+1.5%** on the dive habit - the biggest figure this line has ever read. The counters
say why it is *not* the reason I expected: the gun comes up and is spent 399 times a quarter-hour on
the get-out habit and **419** on the panic habit - *more* often, dashing at everything. So the gain is
in what the heavy pulls land on, not how often they fire, and that mechanism is written in the row as
inferred from two columns rather than measured. No number on the row moved.

### Things that surprised me
- **The window moves this measure more than the radius does.** Same radius, same habit: 16.5%/37.0% on
  ten seeds of five minutes (71 presses of the dash) and **36.9%/57.1%** on eight seeds of two
  minutes (10 presses). A short batch is nothing but the opening knot - the ship is in a pack whenever
  it dashes - and a long one also counts every dash spent on the lone body that brushed past. That
  swing is bigger than the whole distance from 72 px to 150 px, so a radius moved on one batch's
  reading would be a radius moved on the window. Hence **`MIN_PRESSES` = 25**: the tool refuses to
  verdict a batch that thin (`TOO FEW PRESSES`, and `--strict` exits on it), because the sample is
  *presses* and not frames - 5,000 lit frames out of ten dashes is ten observations.
- **Falsifying a check against history instead of against a mutation.** The best test in the new file
  feeds `verdictOf` session 42's own three numbers (72 → 2.0%/13.4%, 110 → 6.4%/30.2%, 150 →
  17.5%/43.8%) and asserts the tool agrees with the session: 110 passes, 72 fails the floor, 150 fails
  the ceiling. If the thresholds drift away from the argument that set them, that test goes red without
  anybody having to mutate a constant, and it is the only kind of test that can catch a promise that
  has quietly become a formality.
- **`quarryFor` is re-askable**, which is the whole reason a radius can be swept without touching the
  sim: `game/enemies.js` hands each walk its quarry and forgets it, and the tool asks the same
  question one step later against whatever `bait` it has just written into `BALANCE`. Cheaper and
  better than a counter in `src/` would have been - and the one case where a counter *was* the right
  call is the overcharge one, because "how often did the run really load the gun" is a fact about a
  run and not about a probe.
- **A charged pull counts as a step of loaded time even though it spends the charge on that step.**
  Deliberate and tested: the sim steps `player.js` (which loads) before `weapons.js` (which spends),
  so the gun really was loaded when the trigger was looked at. Said in the source, because the other
  order is a defensible reading and someone will try it.
- The edit tool's all-or-nothing multi-hunk behaviour bit **three times** (typos in `oldText`, one
  apostrophe inside a single-quoted string - session 112's lesson, learned again), and `git diff
  --stat` before writing anything more was the whole remedy each time.
- 32 cores meant four long batches could run at once and none of them noticed; `tools/line-ab.js
  --stats` is how you find out a stat exists, and it happily printed two that were written this
  morning.

### Decisions, so nobody relitigates them
- **`bait` is not moved on a measure whose noise exceeds its effect.** If somebody wants to move it,
  the honest way is with eyes on a screen, not with a fourth window length.
- **The rank ladder is the thing the re-read put in question, not the radius** - 35.7% at rank 3
  against 37.0% at rank 5 means the fifth card is nearly free of effect. Written up as a new PLAN
  item, with the two ways out (spread the images down more than the dash's own 220 px, or sell the rank
  as the two seconds, which is PLAN's number and would have to be argued out of existence first) and
  the reason it is not this session's to take: both are feel decisions.
- **`weight: 5` is a wager and not a rate.** The row now says so in those words, because the two
  instruments disagree by a factor of twenty and neither is wrong.
- **`overchargeLoaded` counts steps of the game's own clock** (120 a second), not frames. `tether
  .steps` and `turret.steps` already meant that; a third reader of the same kind should not mean
  something else.

### What should come next
1. **Release 1.0.0.** It is the only milestone-10 item left that this project can do alone. The other
   one - "the browser half of the performance pass" - is not: there is no browser on this box and no
   canvas to time, and it has been carried in PLAN as an item *the owner* must take. Before cutting
   1.0.0, say so in NOTES and leave the item where it is with a sentence about who has to do it, and
   re-check the two things the release wants: `tools/alloc-probe.js`'s budgets (session 115's warm
   numbers, tightened in 116 to `STEP_BYTES` 896 / `BODY_BYTES` 5) and `tools/perf-probe.js`'s paint
   budgets, both of which pass today.
2. The **new After-1.0 item**: the afterimage's flat top of the ladder. Needs a screen.
3. Still owed from earlier sessions and unchanged: the difficulty band stays a FAIL by measured
   decision (`tools/difficulty-arc.js`), `tools/gun-tune.js` from session 96, `cageWall` is a thin wall
   for a protanope (deliberately unjudged), and the crowd pairs that share a colour want silhouettes -
   all of them art or judgement jobs a headless session cannot finish honestly.

## Session 118 — The plan is finished. Released 1.0.0

**Released v1.0.0**, the last milestone-10 item this project can take by itself. Nothing in `src/` moved:
the session was the release itself, plus writing down what the release is.

What the item asked for before cutting it was the two budgets, and both were re-read this session rather
than trusted from session 116:

- `tools/alloc-probe.js` — **PASS**, 4 gated loads: the schedule at full crowd 404 B a step, the endless
  wall 515 B, that crowd dying **735 B** (the dearest gated step) against `STEP_BYTES` 896, spread out
  499 B, and PLAN section 2's impossible scene 3.3 KB / 5 B a body against `BODY_BYTES` 5. The empty
  arena is 64 B, which is the floor every one of those numbers is measured from.
- `tools/perf-probe.js` — **PASS**, 4 gated scenes: the worst step **0.103 ms** against 1.5, the dearest
  mean **3,407 canvas operations** against 4,000 and the dearest single frame 3,642 against 4,400.
- `node --test` — 2,043 pass, 0 fail, 2m11s. `node tools/simulate.js` — a full run to the cap, no throw.
  `tools/shake-meter.js` ran inside `release.sh`: the median run sat still 100% of frames against the 95%
  it needs.

Then the CHANGELOG entry, which is the part that took the care. **A release note is a set of claims with no
test behind it**, so every number in it was looked up in the source rather than remembered, and two of my
first guesses were wrong: `BALANCE.ships` has six keys but only **five ships** (`default` is the row the
others are written against, and `hangar.js` says so — "four of the five ships" you can buy), and
`BALANCE.weapons` has seven keys but only **five guns** (likewise `default`, plus `rateMax`, which is a cap
and not a weapon). The rest, stated so the next session can re-check them: **19 upgrade lines**, **9 kinds**
of enemy, **3 bosses** — `bosses.schedule` puts the Warden at 300 s, the Hive at 600 and the Eclipse at 900,
so the scheduled run is fifteen minutes and the win is the Eclipse coming down — and **96 releases** were
out before this one, every one of them still playable from the menu.

PLAN got two edits. `- [ ] Release 1.0.0` is ticked with what it was checked against, so nobody has to
wonder whether it was waved through. And the item that stays open — *the browser half of the performance
pass* — now says out loud that it is the owner's: it wants the F3 plate put up on a real screen and flown to
`bodies 200 / 200`, and there is no browser on this box. That is the only unchecked box in milestones 0–10,
and it is unchecked because of where the work happens and not because anything is unfinished that can be
finished here.

The reference run (`--seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session 117's again — 10m00s / 73,982 /
level 57 / 3,934 kills / 4,934 shards, 7 vacuums, 2,036 in — which is the proof a release that touches no
`game/` file wanted: the same bytes, and now ninety-seven builds of them to choose from in the menu.

### Things that surprised me
- `release.sh` stamped this release itself: **+817 −3** lines since `v0.10.20` (which is session 117's work,
  all of it in `tools/` and `test/` plus the two overcharge counters and the balance rows), with the session
  log at 41,619,607 bytes. The stamping added for the menu has now carried four releases without a complaint.
- Writing the entry found one loose number in the tooling, not in the game: the paint gate is a **mean** of
  4,000 and a **worst frame** of 4,400, and my first line quoted the dearest worst frame against the mean
  budget. The entry now quotes the mean against the mean. Said because it is the kind of slip a changelog is
  full of everywhere, and the only defence is looking each number up where it lives.

### Decisions, so nobody relitigates them
- **1.0.0 and not 0.10.21.** AGENTS.md's `0.<milestone>.<patch>` is how the versions grew *through* the
  milestones; PLAN's own item named this release `1.0.0`, and the event is the milestone list ending. From
  here: **`1.0.<patch>` for fixes and measured retunes, `1.<minor>.0` for a feature that deserves its own
  number** — the After-1.0 list is feature work, so it will start asking that question soon.
- **The entry says the difficulty band was measured, not that it passed.** `tools/difficulty-arc.js` still
  exits FAIL on the careless-build death window, deliberately and with the argument written in the row
  (session 99-ish, repeated in the item). A 1.0 note that claimed the arc was inside PLAN's band would be
  the first false thing in this file, so it doesn't.

### What should come next
1. **The After-1.0 list needs an item a headless session can actually finish.** Everything currently written
   there is either done or waiting for a screen (the afterimage's flat top of the ladder, session 117). Of
   PLAN's suggested ideas the one that is buildable *and* checkable from here is **challenge modifiers** —
   double speed, one hull, no dash: each is a row in `BALANCE` plus a flag the sim can set, and the bot
   already gives a fair yardstick (does the careless build die sooner, by how much, and does the careful one
   still stand?). Write it as a PLAN item first, as the After-1.0 section asks.
2. A **fourth boss** is the other big thing that could be built blind, but it is a piece of *art* as much as a
   machine: `bosses.js` is 2,000 lines of beats and the plan's pillar is that a boss is a pattern you learn by
   eye. It wants a session that can look at it.
3. Still owed and unchanged from session 117's list: the difficulty band's FAIL by decision, `tools/gun-tune.js`
   from session 96, `cageWall` as a thin wall for a protanope, and the crowd pairs that share a colour wanting
   silhouettes. All four want eyes on a screen.

## Session 119 — The first After-1.0 feature: three harder rules, and the ladder that prices them. Released 1.1.0

**Released v1.1.0**: challenge modifiers. `X` cycles the *next* run between nothing, **ONE HULL**, **NO
DASH** and **SWIFT CROWD** (a 1.4x crowd and 1.4x enemy shot speed), one rule at a time. This is the item
session 118 wrote into PLAN's After-1.0 list, and it is the first feature to get its own minor number under
the version rule that session wrote too.

### What shipped
- `src/game/challenges.js` — the whole rule set in one file, in the split `game/perks.js` uses: the table
  (`CHALLENGES`: id, name, sentence), the cycle, four levers, and the words. `BALANCE.challenges` is the
  number sheet (`brittle.hull`, `grounded.dash`, `swift.speedMul`, and `gatedOn`, which lines a rule makes
  pointless). Nothing is cached into a ship: each lever is asked *where the number it changes is already
  read* — `run.js` after the ship's row and the hangar's plating have written the hull, `player.js`
  `beginDash` where a dash is granted, `kinds.js` `makeEnemy` and `enemyshots.js` `enemyShotAt` where a
  speed and a velocity are worked out, `upgrades.js` `linesWithRoom` and `guaranteeSomethingNew` where the
  deck is filtered for a card the run cannot spend. With no rule flying every lever answers its neutral
  number, and that is why `tools/simulate.js` is **byte for byte 1.0.0's** (checked against a `git worktree`
  of HEAD, not from memory: seed 1, 10m00s, score 73,399, level 56, 3,890 kills, build 4/3/3/3/3/4/…).
- Said out loud in five places, because a rule the player forgot is a rule the game cheated with: the title's
  own column, the HUD beside the clock (pink — the arena's colour for the thing that hurts you, not the gold
  of ENDLESS or the dim blue of the day), the pause's rack, and both ending cards. Empty means no rule and an
  empty line takes its space with it, so an ordinary screen is the screen it always was. Under NO DASH the
  dash's ready ring is not drawn at all: a ring promising a jump that never arrives is a lie told sixty times
  a second.
- `tools/challenge-cost.js` — the ladder. Same seeds flown under each rule, careless hand (`--bot human
  --picks random`, pressing the shipped get-out dash), and a **verdict** rather than a table: a rule has to
  beat 0.95x plain's middle score or it is reported as a flavour setting, and a rule that lets the batch
  *outlive* plain fails whatever it scored. `verdictOf` is exported behind the `isMain` guard and
  `test/challenge-cost.test.mjs` asserts on it with made-up rows, so the decision is testable without
  minutes of simming (the shape `tools/ghost-grid.js` settled on).
- `test/challenges.test.mjs` — 21 checks: the table and its words, the cycle, each lever moving exactly its
  own number, the two dash lines leaving the deck, the hull override standing over both the ship's row and
  five ranks of plating, the title line, the HUD mark, both cards, the pause row, the key, and the headless
  door. 26 new checks in all; **2,069 pass, 0 fail** (from 2,043).

### The measurements (`node tools/challenge-cost.js`, 8 seeds × 5m, careless hand)
| rule | middle death | died | middle score | vs plain | hulls lost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| plain | 3m53s | 6/8 | 7,035 | 1.00x | 28 |
| ONE HULL | 1m57s | 8/8 | 2,768 | **0.39x** | 8 |
| NO DASH | 3m03s | 5/8 | 9,650 | 1.37x | 40 |
| SWIFT CROWD | 2m53s | 8/8 | 3,192 | **0.45x** | 24 |

Both judged rules are paid for in the score column and both die sooner, which is the pair the verdict asks
for. NO DASH reads *better* than plain for this hand and is reported and never judged — see the decision
below. `hulls` is the column that says whether the ladder could see a rule at all: an aware bot finishes a
5m run with hull to spare, so it is blind to ONE HULL and the tool says `not measurable on this ladder`
instead of passing a rule it never touched. `--speed` sweeps the swift multiplier without touching a source
file, because the sim reads `BALANCE.challenges.swift.speedMul` every time it builds a body.

Machine cost is unchanged where it could have moved: `tools/alloc-probe.js` **PASS** (dearest gated step
764 B), `tools/perf-probe.js` **PASS** (worst step 0.113 ms against 1.5, dearest mean 3,407 operations
against 4,000), `tools/shake-meter.js` inside `release.sh` still 100% still against the 95% it needs.

### Things that surprised me
- **A test file that calls `game.stop()` at top level breaks every test in the file, silently, and the
  failure looks like a game bug.** Mine ran the stop at the bottom of the module — which is *before* `test()`
  bodies run, because the file body is evaluated first — so the frame loop was dead and every run in the file
  had 0 steps, 0 enemies and `t` 0 forever. Two hours of suspicion about `chooseChallenge` were two hours
  about one line in my own test file. The fix is one line (`stop()` inside a test, or not at all, which is what
  `test/daily.test.mjs` does) and the lesson is bigger than the bug: **when a fresh test file says the sim did
  nothing, look at the file's own top level before you look at the sim.** Three other test files call
  `game.stop()`, always inside a test body, so nothing else was sitting on this.
- Diagnosing it needed a bisect that could not be done by editing the file, so I made throwaway copies in
  `.scratch/` and diffed behaviour between two near-identical files. Worth knowing that trick exists: `.scratch/`
  is gitignored and `node --test .scratch/x.test.mjs` works.
- `world.perkRanks` and not `world.perks` — the plating ranks are `perkRanks` on the world (`game/perks.js`
  `rankOf` reads that). My test guessed the shorter name and got `undefined` for a rank.
- The key-count tests caught the new control exactly as designed: `test/keymap.test.mjs` prints the whole
  shipped table, and `test/keys.test.mjs` counts the rack's rows, walks to its last row and rebinds every
  one of them onto its own letter. Fourteen rows now. The rebind test had to *drop* `KeyX` from its letter
  list — X belongs to a row now, and binding another row onto it is a swap, which is a different thing for
  the test to be doing.
- Only **two** of the three dash cards are gated on the dash. `tether.js` and `afterimage.js` both measure
  how far a dash has travelled off `player.dashLeft`; `overcharge.js` only refuses to load *while* a dash is
  in progress, so it works perfectly well for a ship that cannot jump. `gatedOn.grounded` is those two ids and
  no third, and the synergies needed no handling: a synergy is dealt only when `needsMet` has the run holding
  the base line, and a base line that is never dealt can never be held.

### Decisions, so nobody relitigates them
- **One rule at a time, not a stack.** Combinations multiply into rules nobody measured. A combination, when
  it is wanted, is its own row with its own yardstick.
- **The choice lives for the visit, not in the save** — exactly like `world.ship` and `world.weapon`. A saved
  challenge is a game that is secretly harder for somebody who switched it on weeks ago, and the only cure
  for a rule nobody remembers is a rule nobody can leave set.
- **X answers on the title and on the death's card, and nowhere else.** Not mid-run, not while held, not over
  a card table, and not on the win's card: a won run can be *resumed*, and changing its rules under it would
  be rewriting a fight that was already fought. `main.js`'s `onChallenge` says all of this above itself.
- **NO DASH is reported and never judged**, in the tool and not just in prose: `verdictOf` prints the ratio
  and holds back the verdict, because what a jump is worth is a question about a person's hands and the bot
  presses it a handful of times a quarter hour. Passing it on the bot's 1.37x would have been the tool lying;
  failing it would have been the tool pretending to be a player.
- **The swift crowd speeds bodies and enemy shots, and not a boss's beats.** A telegraph sped up is a pattern
  nobody can learn, and "learn the pattern" is the pillar this rule must not lean on.
- **A rule has to beat 0.95x plain** (`MIN_COST` 0.05 in the tool). The batches are paired on identical seeds,
  so that number is not a noise allowance, it is the claim that a rule which costs a run less than a
  twentieth of its score is not the rule its card says it is.
- **A record per challenge stayed out**, as the PLAN item says: a best under each line wants a save section
  and a panel of its own, and that is the next item, not a fourth lever on these three.

### What should come next
1. **A best per rule**, the way the day keeps its own (`game/daily.js`): a save section, a line on the title
   under the choice, and a row in the standings rack. It is the natural completion of this and it is entirely
   buildable headless — the seed, the rule and the window are all three already in `stats()`.
2. **More rules, each with its own row and its own ladder**: a crowd that grows between the bosses, a hull that
   will not heal (an elite's gift and the leech both spend into nothing), a schedule that skips the second
   boss so the Eclipse arrives at 5m. The frame now costs one `BALANCE.challenges` row, one lever and one
   `CHALLENGES` entry each, so the next one is cheap; the ladder is the work, and it already knows how to
   refuse a rule it cannot see.
3. The four items still owed to a screen, unchanged from session 118: the browser half of the performance
   pass (F3 plate against `bodies 200 / 200`), the difficulty band's deliberate FAIL, `tools/gun-tune.js`,
   `cageWall` as a thin wall for a protanope, and silhouettes for the crowd pairs that share a colour.

## Session 120 — A best under each rule: the save keeps a score per challenge, and says it in three places. Released 1.2.0

**Released v1.2.0**: the record half of the challenge rules. Every rule now has a number of its own — the
best this save has flown *under* it — which is what turns a rule from a difficulty dial into something to
beat. This is the item session 119 wrote into PLAN as "a separate item, because it wants a save section and
a panel of its own", and it is the first thing built on top of 1.0's own feature list.

### What shipped
- `SAVE.challenges.bests` — one map, rule id → best score, in `core/save.js`'s existing `counts` shape (the
  one the perk tally uses), with the **score's** ceiling on the number side and not a rank's: a best under a
  rule is the same kind of number as `score.best`, and `MAX_COUNT` 1,000 would have been a record nobody
  could beat. One map rather than a key per rule is what keeps a fourth rule a row in a table instead of a
  request for storage. A rule missing from the map has never been flown, which is an answer and not a hole —
  `bestOf` says 0 and every line that would have printed it prints nothing instead.
- `src/game/challenges.js` grew the third section it always had room for: **the records** (`bestsFromSave`,
  `bestOf`, `bankChallenge`) and the words that say them. `bankChallenge` is called from `bankRun` after the
  all-time best and the day's, as the narrowest of the three claims, and it keeps the same bargain they keep
  about a run that is won, handed back and finally goes down: the second ending only wins if the run came out
  bigger. `world.newChallengeBest` is the per-run flag, cleared in `resetRun` beside `newDailyBest`.
- Said in three places, and nowhere a step has to look: the **title's rule line** ends with `1,234 BEST FOR
  THIS RULE` when the save has one (so the key that sets a rule shows what that rule is worth — which is the
  whole point of the feature), and an **ending's card** ends with the same number or with `NEW BEST FOR THIS
  RULE`, which is exactly the pair `game/daily.js` makes about the day. Both go through one private
  `recordWords`, so a card and a title cannot describe the same number differently. `FOR THIS RULE` is not
  padding: a card has an all-time BEST a hand's width above it and would otherwise say BEST twice with two
  different numbers.
- **The codex's fifth rack, HARDER RULES** (`showRules`, `index.html #ruleRow`, painted at boot and by every
  ending like the log and the awards). One row per rule in the order the key cycles them — its number and its
  sentence, or `NOT FLOWN YET` and no glow, wearing the codex's own `unknown` class. The sentence is on every
  row, flown or not, because this is the one place all three rules can be read at once instead of cycled
  blind.
- `tools/headless/harness.js` — `ruleRow` in the stub page and `screen.rules` in the snapshot, in the
  `entryRow` shape because a rule row can be dim.
- `test/challenge-records.test.mjs` — 18 checks: the ledger round-tripping through the save, what the store
  refuses to write (a score that is a sentence, a score that is a fraction, a score below zero, an id the
  game cannot name, a ledger that is a word), what `bankChallenge` decides (no rule, first run, smaller
  second ending, bigger one, zero, and a rule that is not this rule), every combination of the words with and
  without a record, a real visit banking and lighting the card, the title after `X`, the rack's rows, the rack
  repainted by the ending that changed it without the panel being opened again, and that a flying run writes
  nothing to storage while its ending does. **2,087 pass, 0 fail** (from 2,069).

### A rack and not a panel — the one place PLAN was overruled
PLAN said "a panel of its own". Three rules do not earn a third key when the panel that already answers
"what has this save flown" is one press away, and the codex's fourth rack (the log) had already broken out of
"met n of 30" to be exactly that question. So the record went there: read and not bought, one row per rule,
same row shape, same `fitPanel` fitting. If a fourth and fifth rule arrive the rack grows by a row, which is
cheap; a panel would have wanted a key, a hint line, a `panels` entry and a fit test for three rows.

### The measurements
- Reference run **byte for byte unchanged**, checked against a `git worktree` of HEAD~1 and not from memory:
  seed 1 → 10m00s, 73,399, level 56, 3,890 kills; seed 20261006 → 73,982, level 57, 3,934 kills. Both
  `diff`s empty. An ordinary run never calls `bankChallenge` at all, which is the whole reason this holds.
- `tools/alloc-probe.js` **PASS** (4 gated loads, dearest step 735 B, a body 2 B a step), `tools/perf-probe.js`
  **PASS** (worst step 0.105 ms, dearest mean 3,407 operations), and `tools/shake-meter.js` inside
  `release.sh` still 100% still against the 95% it needs.

### Things that surprised me
- **`test/alloc-probe.test.mjs` had been failing one run in five, and it was not my change.** The suite got a
  red test the first time I ran it and I assumed I had put an allocation in a walk; a clean `git worktree` of
  HEAD failed it too, twice in five runs. "All three together is the crowd" bounded the cost of 900 sparks and
  60 shots *on top of* the crowd as a ratio — `both < crowd × 1.35` — and the two numbers it divides do not
  move together: 38-42 B on a quiet box (1.11x) against **117-121 B** with eight test files running at once
  (1.36x, and a failure). It is bounded in bytes now, like the check directly above it: what each pool lives in
  is allowed on its own, doubled — 192 B against the 38-121 measured, while a real regression (an object per
  spark) is thousands. **Do not "tighten" this back to a ratio**: the ratio was the bug, and the noise is the
  machine, not the game.
- Adding a save section costs two edits in `test/save.test.mjs` — the fresh-document shape and the
  hard-coded key-order list that proves the document is written in schema order. Both are worth having; both
  will bite whoever adds section fourteen.
- Two assertions in `test/challenges.test.mjs` pinned the title line and the card line word for word, and both
  failed the moment the record was appended — which was the cheapest possible proof that the feature works from
  end to end. They now check the *rule* part word for word and delegate the record to the new file; the words
  test also writes an empty ledger first, because "a rule with no record" is a state of the save and the file
  should not be hoping for it by ordering.
- `STATE.OVER` is 2, not 4. A launch press that is refused by the restart guard leaves the game in 2 and the
  failure reads like a mystery level-up; the fix was `frames(GUARD)` before the press, which is what
  `test/daily.test.mjs` has always done.
- The title's rule line is painted by `X` and at boot and by nothing in between, so it would have gone one run
  stale the moment a record could exist. `showGameOver` and `showVictory` repaint it from the summary the way
  they already repaint `showStanding` — nothing can see the title from under a card, but a line that is a run
  behind is the sort of thing that gets a panel lying later.

### Decisions, so nobody relitigates them
- **Per rule, not per rule-and-ship, not per rule-and-seed.** A record per (rule, ship) is fifteen numbers, most
  of them about a ship nobody flies on purpose, and the point of the record is "what is this *rule* worth to
  you". The ship is on the card already when it matters.
- **The pause says nothing about the record**, exactly as the pause says nothing about the day's best: the pause
  rack is about the run that is being held, and the record is about the save.
- **The record travels with the card** (`summary.challengeBests`, `newChallengeBest`) rather than being read
  off the save inside `ui/screens.js`, for the same reason the codex ledger and the log do — the panel that
  goes up over a card must not be able to disagree with it.
- **Read at endings and at title paints, never in a step.** `core/save.js` re-reads storage on every call by
  design; a record asked during `stepWorld` would be a JSON parse sixty times a second. There is a test for
  this (`the ledger is written at an ending and never while a run is flying`).
- **A run that scored nothing banks nothing** — no rule ever shows a 0 as though somebody had scored it, which
  is the same reason the title's TODAY number stays hidden until the day has been flown.

### What should come next
1. **The log does not say which rule a run was flown under** — new PLAN item, and it is real: a 90,000 scored
   on ONE HULL sits in the PAST RUNS column next to a 90,000 flown plain. It is not a patch, because
   `core/save.js` `records` judges a row whole and a new required field would silently drop every row on every
   existing save. Either the store grows an honest "optional field" kind or the log is rewritten once on the
   way in. The hazard is written into PLAN so the next session does not discover it by breaking somebody's save.
2. **More rules**, each with its own row and its own ladder (`tools/challenge-cost.js` already refuses to judge
   a rule it cannot see). They now come with a record for free, which they would not have before this session.
3. The four items still owed to a screen, unchanged from session 119: the browser half of the performance pass
   (F3 plate against `bodies 200 / 200`), the difficulty band's deliberate FAIL, `tools/gun-tune.js`,
   `cageWall` as a thin wall for a protanope, and silhouettes for the crowd pairs that share a colour.

## Session 121 — The run log says which rule a run was flown under, and the save grew a field it is allowed to lack. Released 1.2.1

**Released v1.2.1**: the second half of the item session 120 left open. A row of the codex's PAST RUNS rack
read `WISP · 40s · 90,000` whether the run stood on one hull or three, which is the exact thing the harder
rules were written to stop - a score quoted without its units. Now it reads
`WISP · 40s · 90,000 · ONE HULL`, and a plain row says nothing because it had nothing.

The PLAN item said this was "store work with a migration in it", and it was half right: the store did grow a
kind, and the migration turned out to be the half that could be thrown away.

### What shipped
- `core/save.js` grew **`KINDS.optional(inner)`**, the honest answer to "a field a row written before it
  existed is allowed to lack". It wraps another kind, and `records` reads the marker it hangs off the
  function: an absent field is **left off the record** rather than filled with a stand-in, and the reader that
  owns the field says what absent means. A value that *is* there is judged by `inner` like any other, so
  "allowed to be absent" is nowhere near "allowed to be nonsense" - `rule: 'ONE HULL'`, `rule: ''`,
  `rule: null` and `rule: 4` each condemn their row and leave their neighbours alone.
- `RUN_FIELDS` grew a sixth field, `rule: KINDS.optional(KINDS.name)`, and it is the only optional field in
  the document. It holds game/challenges.js's **id** and not its display name, for the same reason the hangar
  stores ship ids: the words belong to the table and can be reworded, the id is what a row means.
- `game/history.js`'s `recordOf` asks `activeOf(world)` and writes the key **only when there is a rule**. That
  is the whole trick: a plain run's row is byte for byte `{"seed":…,"won":false}` as it ever was, and a row
  written before rules existed reads back as exactly that same row - so there is no migration, no version
  bump, and no first-read write that would break the store's own "a read never destroys" promise.
- `ui/screens.js`: `logLine` puts the rule **next to the score** (it is the score's units) and `CLEARED` still
  comes last; a new `logRule` says nothing at all for a row without one, and names an unrecognised id by its
  own text exactly as `logShip` has always done for a ship this page has never met - a save is allowed to be
  newer than the page reading it. `LOG_DOT` came out of the three inline copies of `'   ·   '` while I was in
  there, for the same reason `logShip` exists: one join, said once.
- Tests, one at each layer the change touches: `test/save.test.mjs` (predecessor rows read whole and stay
  without a rule, four kinds of rubbish refused, and the *written text* of a plain row proved byte for byte),
  `test/history-rules.test.mjs` (a ruled run's row keeps its rule while the plain run above it has none, and
  the document round-trips both), `test/history.test.mjs` (a real visit: rule on, rule off, both rows in the
  save), and `test/history-saved.test.mjs` now **arrives** with a ruled row and a row under a rule that does
  not exist in this build, and prints both.

### Decisions, so nobody relitigates them
- **Absence, not a word for "none".** The alternative PLAN offered - rewrite the log once on the way in with
  `rule: ''` or `rule: 'plain'` filled in - costs a migration, a write on a read, and a sentinel the store has
  to be taught to accept (`''` is not a `NAME` and never will be). It also makes a rack that *lies by
  omission* the other way: a plain row would have to say PLAIN, and every row that predates the field would
  say it too, about a rule nobody was flying because it did not exist. The absence is the answer, which is how
  `keys.binds` already spells "this control is on its shipped key".
- **`''` is refused as a stored rule on purpose.** The game's own vocabulary for "no rule" is `''`
  (game/challenges.js), so it is tempting to let it through. It would mean the same fact spelled two ways -
  no key, or an empty one - and every reader would have to check both. A plain row writes no key, full stop.
- **The id travels; the name is looked up.** A reworded rule (`ONE HULL` → `BRITTLE`) rewords old rows with
  it, which is right: it is the same rule. A rule *renamed by id* is a different rule and would want its own
  row, which is what `challenges.js`'s `nameOf('') === ''` and `logRule`'s fallback are there to make loud
  rather than wrong.
- **The rack, not the pause and not the card.** Both of those already said the rule (sessions 119 and 120).
  The log was the one place a run's number outlived its units.

### The measurements
- Reference run **untouched**: `tools/simulate.js --trace --seed 20261006` diffs empty against a
  `git worktree` of the previous commit, and the plain numbers still read 73,982 / level 57 / 3,934 kills
  (seed 1: 73,399 / 56 / 3,890). A mirror written at endings and never in a step is supposed to do exactly
  this, and `recordOf` gained one `activeOf` call per ending to do it.
- **2,090 tests pass, 0 fail** (from 2,087). `tools/alloc-probe.js` PASS (4 gated loads, dearest step 761 B),
  `tools/perf-probe.js` PASS (worst step 0.115 ms, dearest mean 3,407 operations), the stillness check in
  `release.sh` still 100% against the 95% it needs.

### Things that surprised me
- **A new record field costs nothing at read time only because `records` builds the row it returns field by
  field.** It does not copy the object, so an absent optional field simply never appears - I had braced for
  having to delete a key back off. The one place that assumption could leak is `normalise`, which copies a
  section key when `value !== null`; a top-level optional field would have written `key: undefined` into the
  document. It skips `undefined` too now, with a line saying why, because `KINDS.optional` exists and the
  next person will reach for it at the top level sooner or later.
- **`playOneRun` inherits the rule the last run chose.** My new visit test flew a plain run after a ruled one
  and got a second `brittle` row, because `world.challenge` outlives a run on purpose (it is a choice about
  the *next* run, like the ship pick). The test now says `challenge: ''` out loud, which is the same lesson
  tools/challenge-cost.js learned last session - a tool that forgets the pick is sticky measures the same rule
  twice and calls it a control.
- Two of the awkward-row indices in `test/history-saved.test.mjs` are hard-coded numbers into `AWKWARD`, so
  adding rows to that array moves them; one assertion there wanted `[4]` and really wanted `[5]`. Worth
  knowing before somebody else adds a fourth awkward case.
- `index.html`'s comment on the codex's racks claims the log's rows are "numbers and short words" and needs no
  width cap of its own. A rule word plus `CLEARED` on the same row is closer to the edge than before - it
  wraps under itself inside the 34ch column, which is what `.entry`'s `flex-wrap` is for - so the claim still
  holds, but it is now a claim about four facts on a line and not three.

### What should come next
1. **More rules.** They now come with a record *and* a logged row for free, which they would not have had
   before session 120 and 121. `tools/challenge-cost.js` still refuses to judge a rule it cannot see, and a
   fourth rule is now one row in each of two tables plus one `CHALLENGES` line.
2. **Optional fields are available now**, so any other record in the document can grow. There is only one
   record shape today (`runs.log`); if a second one appears - a per-day history, a replay index - it should
   be built with `optional` on anything that might arrive later, from the start.
3. The four items still owed to a screen, unchanged from session 119: the browser half of the performance pass
   (F3 plate against `bodies 200 / 200`), the difficulty band's deliberate FAIL, `tools/gun-tune.js`,
   `cageWall` as a thin wall for a protanope, and silhouettes for the crowd pairs that share a colour.
4. The afterimage's fourth and fifth ranks still buy very little over its third (PLAN's open item). It wants a
   decision about how a card feels, and this session did not grow eyes for that either.

## Session 122 — A fourth rule: THICK CROWD, and the ladder that could not choose its number. Released 1.3.0

Suite **2,090 → 2,099** (7 new in `test/challenge-thick.test.mjs`, 1 in `test/challenge-cost.test.mjs`,
and one new check in `test/challenges.test.mjs` that every rule written with an empty `says` has a
builder). The reference run (`tools/simulate.js --seed 20261006 --trace`) is byte for byte session 121's
again - diffed against a `git worktree` of HEAD, not remembered - because with no rule flying the new
lever answers 1 and multiplying a budget by 1 does not even round.

**Released v1.3.0**: the fourth challenge rule. `X` now cycles nothing, ONE HULL, NO DASH, SWIFT CROWD
and **THICK CROWD** - the arena holds half again as much of the crowd as it ships.

### What shipped
`BALANCE.challenges.thick = { holdMul: 1.5 }` and one lever, `crowdHoldOf(world)`, spent in the two
places the arena's two walls are already read: `waves.js` `crowdBudget` multiplies the schedule's
terms, and `bodyCeiling` its wall on standing bodies. One number and not two because the walls are
already tuned to meet - `crowdMax` 400 points is ~89 bodies at the crowd's 4.5 points a body and
`maxBodies` is 100 - so moving one alone would only promote the quieter one to being the rule. The
*endless* wall (`endless.growth.bodiesCeil`, 200) is deliberately outside the multiply and still the
outer wall: it is a frame budget that has been timed on a real frame and a challenge may not move it.

Everything the last three rules' machinery already did came free, which is what sessions 119-121 were
buying: a best under the rule on the title and the card, its row on the codex's HARDER RULES rack, its
word beside the score in PAST RUNS, the pink mark by the clock and the line on the pause's rack. The one
piece of generalising needed was `saysOf`: SWIFT CROWD's sentence was built out of its own number and so
is the new one's, so what had been an inline `if` is a `SENTENCES` table now, and a rule added later with
an empty `says` and no builder has a test that says so instead of printing a name with nothing under it.

### The measurements (`node tools/challenge-cost.js`, careless hand unless said)
| rule | middle death | died | middle score | vs plain | hulls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| plain | 3m53s | 6/8 | 7,035 | 1.00x | 28 |
| THICK CROWD 1.5 | 2m48s | 6/8 | 4,211 | **0.60x** | 26 |
| THICK CROWD, careful hand | - | 0/8 | 20,455 | **0.73x** | 11 against plain's 3 |

The careful hand is the interesting row: nobody dies under the rule and it still costs a run - a hand
